items.description: The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved a $213.5 million class-action settlement against Sun Life.

items._ogDesc: The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved a $213.5 million class-action settlement against Sun Life.
items.body:
TORONTO — The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved a $213.5 million class-action settlement against Sun Life.

A news release from law firm Kim Spencer McPhee Barristers P.C. says the action began in 2010 regarding alleged improper administration of three universal life insurance policies, including Universal Plus, Flexiplus, and OptiMet.

The policies were sold by Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. agents in Canada between 1987 and 1998.

The release says Sunlife has denied any wrongdoing, and the company did not immediately respond to a request for comment after hours.

The law firm says the settlement is the largest reported settlement in any life insurance policy dispute in Canadian history, concerning 70,000 eligible current and former Flexiplus and Universal Plus policyholders in Canada.

Eldon Fehr, representative plaintiff, says the settlement will provide significant benefits to current and former Sun Life policyholders.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026

items._ogDesc: Mark Carney acknowledged talks had intensified slightly in recent days and Donald Trump and his officials have suggested a deal could be possible before next week midterm elections in the United States.
items.body:
OTTAWA — A Canadian official says there has been “limited progress” made in recent trade talks with the United States.

Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday acknowledged talks had intensified slightly in recent days and U.S. President Donald Trump and his officials have suggested a deal could be possible before next week midterm elections in the United States.

But a Canadian government official with knowledge of the negotiations, who was not authorized to speak publicly about them, says today while discussions have continued, “there has been limited progress.”

Diplomatic relations between Canada and the U.S. have been dicey since Carney’s government walked away from formal trade talks in August and the prime minister accused the Americans of making unreasonable last-minute demands.

In response, Washington imposed tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian goods, and Ottawa followed up with retaliatory tariffs on American products.

Trump announced Friday he will lift some of the 50 per cent tariffs on Canada at the end of the month, while adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026

With files from David Baxter in Ottawa and Aaron Sousa in Edmonton

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canada, United Arab Emirates sign defence, energy deals during crown prince’s visit
items.description: Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a handful of trade and infrastructure agreements during the crown prince of Abu Dhabi’s visit to Ottawa on Tuesday.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney greets Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, U.A.E., as he arrives on Parliament Hill in Ottawa during a visit, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a handful of trade and infrastructure agreements during the crown prince of Abu Dhabi’s visit to Ottawa on Tuesday.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a free trade deal on Tuesday they say was reached in a “record” time of 47 days, and have also agreed to start talks on an extradition treaty.

The trade deal was one of a handful of trade and infrastructure agreements signed during the crown prince of Abu Dhabi’s visit to Ottawa on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan to Parliament Hill. The crown prince’s motorcade was escorted onto the Hill by four RCMP horses.

It’s just the latest example of the Carney government’s outreach to nations with questionable human rights records as it works to redirect Canada’s trade around an increasingly erratic United States.

Carney was in Turkey last week to discuss deeper economic and social ties with the NATO ally. In recent months, Turkish authorities have targeted multiple LGBTQ+ groups and individuals — detaining dozens of activists, breaking into association offices and raiding popular hangouts.

The UAE has taken on increasing importance in global politics and has been praised for work aimed at ending conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. But the country has been accused of fuelling a militia in Sudan that conducted what Washington has called a genocide — a claim Abu Dhabi denies.

Asked Tuesday about human rights concerns linked to the UAE, International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said “human rights never takes a back seat with Canada.”

“It’s important that we continue to engage, being at those tables to make sure that we raise whatever we need to raise in terms of human rights,” he said.

At home, Human Rights Watch says the UAE is responsible for “rampant systemic human rights violations,” particularly with regard to freedom of speech.

Seventeen civil society organizations signed an open letter earlier this year warning Canada against deeper ties to the UAE and arguing the country is perpetuating the war in Sudan.

The letter, signed by the Trade Justice Network, Amnistie internationale Canada francophone and Equality Fund, said as Canada looks to diversify its trade, it needs to assert support for human rights as a core Canadian value.

“Our prosperity cannot be built at the expense of the lives and futures of the Sudanese people,” said the letter.

Ministers from Canada and the UAE have also signed agreements pledging investments in clean power and energy infrastructure and collaboration on diplomatic training.

They’ve signed an agreement on defence co-operation covering military education and training, joint exercises, cybersecurity and information sharing, as well as the creation of a joint military committee.

Stephanie Kusie, Conservative MP and critic for international trade, said in a social media post Tuesday that it’s “tiresome” to see the prime minister holding “yet another flashy meeting with no tangible outcomes for Canadians, as he did today with the UAE.”

“Instead of another fancy ceremony, Canadians deserve clear information about the number of jobs and the names of projects involved, not another vague ‘strategic partnership’ that lacks any real details on how it would improve their lives,” she said. 

The Prime Minister’s Office said the trade deal will reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99 per cent of current Canadian exports to the UAE once it’s fully implemented.

The office says the agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including those in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental and engineering sectors.

The Prime Minister’s Office said the trade agreement is expected to take effect next year.

During the visit, Canada and the UAE also announced they will launch negotiations on an extradition treaty and a mutual legal assistance treaty.

During a meeting with the crown prince in his West Block office, Carney said the visit would reinforce the countries’ partnership, which has grown substantially over the past year.

At a state dinner for the crown prince hosted by Carney in downtown Ottawa on Monday, the prime minister said the two countries are united in their determination to “build for the future.”

Carney travelled to the United Arab Emirates last year. At the end of that November visit, the prime minister said Ottawa was working on a $1-billion project to expand critical minerals processing capacity in Canada.

At the same time, the UAE pledged to invest about $70 billion in Canada.

Sidhu said Tuesday that sum could include new investments in mining, logistics, energy and digital technology.

“They are actively looking at deploying that as soon as possible,” he said. “They’ll have more to say publicly soon.”

The Prime Minister’s Office said the visit led to “significant progress” on the UAE’s commitment to invest in Canada.

It said Emirati multinational logistics company DP World has signed an agreement with the Arctic Gateway Group and CentrePort Canada to advance trade opportunities and develop a transportation corridor linking the Port of Churchill, the Hudson Bay Railway, CentrePort Canada and DP World’s global logistics network.

It said agreements were signed between renewable energy company Masdar and Natural Resources Canada on green energy projects, and between Invest in Canada and the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce and Industry on sharing information and co-ordinating visits.

The Liberals have set out to double non-U.S. exports over the next decade. The government’s spring economic update said non-U.S. goods and services exports increased by $33 billion in 2025 compared to 2024.

In 2025, Canada’s two-way merchandise trade with the UAE was valued at $3.5 billion, with $2.8 billion in exports and $679.1 million in imports.

-With files from Dylan Robertson

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items.title: Trump congratulates B.C.’s premier-designate on ‘big victory’
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump has congratulated B.C.’s premier-designate on the Conservative party’s election win.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[U.S. President Donald Trump is shown in a photo by the Associated Press (left) B.C.'s premier-designate Lorne Doerkson is shown in a photo by The Canadian Press.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump has congratulated B.C.’s premier-designate on the Conservative party’s election win.
items.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump has congratulated B.C.’s premier-designate on the Conservative party’s election win.

Trump posted to Truth Social Tuesday, sharing an article about the decisive defeat of the B.C. NDP in Saturday’s snap election.

“Congratulations to Lorne Doerkson on his Big Victory. Conservatives are moving strong in Canada! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” the post said.

The B.C. Conservative party won a commanding majority and is set to form government for the first time in nearly a century.

David Eby, who was ousted as premier and resigned as the B.C. NDP’s leader, invoked Trump and the trade war when he called the controversial early election in September.

Eby characterized his Conservative opponents as overly sympathetic to Trump and often accused the party of trying to import “MAGA-style” politics by focusing on culture war issues and offering a haven for candidates with extreme views.

This is the second time the results out of British Columbia have prompted a post from the U.S. president, who shared a story about the win—without offering comment—Sunday.

That day, Doerkson was asked what he thought about the apparent show of support from Trump. The premier-designate said he does not see himself as a Trump ally, and that his loyalty lies with the province and its people.

“I assure you that my commitment, my dedication, is to British Columbia,” he said.

items.title: Canada, EU hope to solidify associate membership details next year, announcement unlikely at upcoming summit
items.description: Ahead of the upcoming Canada-EU Summit in Montreal, European officials say the exact details of an agreement  will not be finalized this week, but that they’re hoping to hammer out those details of Canada’s “associate membership” in the 27-member bloc to make an official announcement next year.

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Ahead of the upcoming Canada-EU Summit in Montreal, European officials say the exact details of an agreement  will not be finalized this week, but that they’re hoping to hammer out those details of Canada’s “associate membership” in the 27-member bloc to make an official announcement next year.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Ahead of the upcoming Canada-EU Summit in Montreal, European officials say the exact details of an agreement will not be finalized this week, but that they’re hoping to hammer out those details of Canada’s “associate membership” in the 27-member bloc to make an official announcement next year.

The officials made the comments in a background briefing to reporters ahead of the summit, set to take place Thursday and Friday, also calling it one of the most important summits the EU has ever held.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made headlines last month when she formally invited Prime Minister Mark Carney to take the Canada-EU relationship to the next level, saying in a state of the union address that she wants to open the door for Canada to be the first “associate member” of the group.

Carney said at the time that Canada is open to the proposition.

The officials briefing reporters on Tuesday, meanwhile, insisted member states are on board with what would be the closest-ever alliance with another country — the closest one could get to the EU without official membership — but conceded there is debate over the name.

They also said they don’t envision a partnership of this kind being offered to others, explaining that there could be two types of deal: an “alliance of the future,” which could be open to other countries, and what is currently being described as “associate membership,” which is being drawn up with only Canada in mind.

The officials said the goal is to have the concept ready for endorsement by the next Canada-EU summit next year.

Speaking to reporters on his way into a cabinet meeting on Parliament Hill Tuesday, Carney said he’s “looking forward” to the summit, adding “a lot of work has gone into this.”

“This is the launch of further formal discussions, negotiations over the course of the next year,” he said.

“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” he added. “What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians, young Canadians in terms of opportunities to study, work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities, Canadian researchers in terms of depths of opportunity, and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation.”

In an interview with CTV Question Period last month, Canada’s Ambassador to the EU Jonathan Wilkinson also said neither side of the talks had landed on what to call the new partnership, whether “associate member” or something else.

“I think it’s totally fair for Canadians to ask, ‘What does it mean?’ It’s totally fair for the Europeans to ask, ‘What does it mean?’ Because it’s quite new for them as well,” Wilkinson told host Vassy Kapelos, when pressed on the potential connotations of the “associate member” name.

“It is actually about a series of initiatives that are focused in areas that are both economically important — from a trade and from a security perspective — but also about enhancing Canada’s overall sovereignty,” he added. “This is about building sovereignty, making ourselves more secure and more sovereign. It’s not about the reverse.”

Some members voice concerns

Some EU members voiced concerns last month when von der Leyen floated the term “associate member” in reference to Canada.

In an interview with CTV Power Play on Tuesday, German Ambassador to Canada Matthias Luttenberg said his country has long supported Canada deepening ties with Europe, but that there are worries about the potential new label.

“If you come up with a new concept in the European Union, and you propose something, be it the Commission or somebody else, then of course it takes some time to reflect for all 27 member states,” Luttenberg told guest host Graham Richardson.

“I think we have been a little surprised by the announcement, which doesn’t mean that we cannot agree on it,” he also said, adding Germany has other concerns because it uses the term “associated membership” in reference to the bloc’s relationship with countries like Ukraine, for example.

The ambassador said he doesn’t believe there was any “bad intention” in proposing the concept, and that Germany’s concerns are not directed at Canada.

“It was certainly a gesture of the best intention, the very good will to bring Canada also verbally as close as possible to the EU,” Luttenberg said.

He said the term used is still up for discussion, and cautioned against anyone getting distracted from the other agenda items at this week’s summit.

The summit is taking place on the 10-year anniversary of the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) being signed. A handful of countries a decade later, however, have still not ratified the deal.

The EU officials in Tuesday’s briefing called CETA a success story, and said they’re working with the remaining member states to ensure ratification.

As Canada seeks to deepen ties with the EU, meanwhile, it’s still embroiled in a trade war with the United States. U.S. President Donald Trump reacted to the potential of Canada’s EU “associate membership” last month, saying it could be considered a “hostile act,” calling it “laughable.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has also weighed in, speaking to reporters ahead of the prime minister’s trip to Europe last month, saying Canada already has trade and defence agreements with the EU, in the form of CETA and NATO.

“We want Canada to have free trade with Europe, co-operation with Europe, but we will never surrender our independence and sovereignty over our laws, our tax money, and our immigration policies,” Poilievre said.

He added the Conservatives want to see “an economic action plan” to support Canadians struggling with the cost of living, rather than an unclear goal of potentially conforming to European systems and policies.

With files from CTV News chief political correspondent Vassy Kapelos

items.title: Ottawa demands plan to restore Stelco jobs before meeting Cleveland-Cliffs CEO
items.description: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is calling on the U.S.-based owner of Stelco Inc. to provide a concrete plan and timeline to restore jobs at its Canadian steel mills.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Stelco steel production facility in Hamilton, Ont., on Monday, Feb. 10, 2025. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Nick Iwanyshyn]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Nick Iwanyshyn</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is calling on the U.S.-based owner of Stelco Inc. to provide a concrete plan and timeline to restore jobs at its Canadian steel mills.
items.body:
CLEVELAND — Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is calling on the U.S.-based owner of Stelco Inc. to provide a concrete plan and timeline to restore jobs at its Canadian steel mills before she will agree to meet with CEO Lourenco Goncalves.

Cleveland-Cliffs said late Monday it’s in full compliance with the promises it made as part of an Investment Canada Act review that allowed its purchase of Stelco in 2024.

The company also said Stelco has requested a meeting between Joly and Goncalves to talk about a path toward resuming full employment for workers who have been temporarily laid off.

Joly said Tuesday that the government wants to see Stelco’s proposed plan to recall laid off workers before she will sit down with the head of Cleveland-Cliffs.

  • Latest updates on company news here

“First and foremost, what I want is a plan to bring back the jobs and I want a timeline,” she told reporters ahead of a cabinet meeting in Ottawa.

“I’m always willing to sit down, but that’s the first condition.”

Joly has accused Cleveland-Cliffs of breaking six binding promises made when it bought Stelco, including a five-year commitment to maintain unionized staffing levels and retain most non-unionized workers.

She said Ottawa could still take the company to court to enforce its commitments, seek financial penalties or require the sale of Stelco.

Cleveland-Cliffs said it’s in full compliance with each of its 34 undertakings, and in several important areas has even gone beyond what it committed to do.

“The facts are clear,” Goncalves said in a statement. “We made serious commitments to Canada when we acquired Stelco, and we have honoured them.”

Cleveland-Cliffs announced plans on Sept. 28 to lay off up to 500 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton Works and Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont., blaming U.S. tariffs, weak demand and an oversupply of imported steel in Canada.

“For galvanized products, the imports of non-automotive galvanized steel that continue to flood the Canadian market remain problematic,” Goncalves said on Monday.

“We want to find a solution for Hamilton and its workers as soon as possible and believe common sense trade policy will make this a reality.”

In response to the company’s claims that Ottawa isn’t doing enough to curb steel dumping, the federal government has pointed to measures aimed at limiting overseas imports, including tighter quotas introduced in December 2025.

Canada also raised tariffs on certain U.S. steel imports, including galvanized steel, to 50 per cent on Sept. 8.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne defended Ottawa’s steel import restrictions Tuesday, despite complaints from Stelco that cheaper foreign steel is continuing to undermine the company’s Hamilton operations.

He said the government is trying to balance steel production with steel consumption in Canada, which he pegged at about 13 million tonnes per year.

But Champagne said Ottawa must also ensure Canadian businesses have access to products that are not manufactured domestically or readily available in certain regions.

“There are certain types of steel, for example, that are not made in Canada (and) you have regional markets,” he told reporters. “In a country as big as Canada ... sometimes you need to import steel to make sure that you would have the supply needed at the time needed in the location needed.”

Champagne added: “You need to support workers, you need support industry and you need also to have these measures to protect the domestic market.”

The steelmaker said Stelco will update its compliance report following the Oct. 31 close of the current reporting period.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

items.title: CTV News asked Georgia voters about tariffs. Their answer was clear
items.description: If you ask Georgia cattle farmer Scott Craig about who has been impacted by the trade war and what costs have gone up, he’ll tell you just about everyone and everything, especially in agriculture.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Trump’s tariffs and war are delivering punishing expenses in the Deep South. Voters tell CTV News it’s testing their support. (Image credits: CTV News, The Associates Press, The Canadian Press)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: If you ask Georgia cattle farmer Scott Craig about who has been impacted by the trade war and what costs have gone up, he’ll tell you just about everyone and everything, especially in agriculture.
items.body:
ATLANTA — If you ask Georgia cattle farmer Scott Craig about who has been impacted by the trade war and what costs have gone up, he’ll tell you just about everyone and everything, especially in agriculture.

“I classify [it] as our three F’s. The fuel, the feed and the fertilizer.”

Craig has been a cattle farmer in McDonough, Ga., about an hour from Atlanta, for most of his life.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“I love being out here with the cows. It’s all I’ve ever done.”

But like many, he’s seen his costs go up from butchering to fuel. Beyond the import costs associated with tariffs, the war in Iran has spiked the cost of gas and diesel. One tracker published by Brown University suggests the price of diesel in Georgia has risen by US$2.18 per gallon (C$0.80 per litre) since the war began.

“It’s more than double to fill up these tractors when we either bush hog or planting or cutting hay or doing anything on them,” he said. “The cost is through the roof now.”

There is solid support for U.S. President Donald Trump in Georgia, but there are also questions about the president’s trade policy. While many are loyal to Trump, voters are divided over the high cost of living.

“I’m sure it’s going to impact people when they vote,” Craig said of the upcoming U.S. midterms.

Replacing Canada’s exports?

It’s a sentiment echoed by Greg Adams, vice president at Adams-Briscoe Seed Co., a feed, seed and farm supply store in Jackson, Ga. He hopes Georgians consider Trump’s trade policies when they cast their ballots in next week’s midterm election.

“I hope it has a bigger impact than it seems. But we are down here in the South, and it’s kind of hard to see past the noise.”

Adams has noticed his costs increase too, especially for fertilizer.

“They can’t get it locally, they can’t source it locally. They have to get it from Canada, and there’s not too many other countries that are putting out the supply that y’all do,” Adams said. “My seed prices are going to go up and I’ve got to pass all that down to my customers.”

Georgians want stability: expert

It’s not just the cost of goods coming in. Canada is Georgia’s largest export market at US$6.8 billion a year. Two-way trade between the state and Canada totalled around US$13.3 billion last year.

Georgia’s manufacturing and agriculture industries are among those in the state that have been hit hard by tariffs. The Georgia Chamber of Commerce said some businesses are delaying decisions around investment and expansion.

“The stable trade environment is what so many Georgia businesses are looking for,” said Daniela Perry, the executive director of the Georgia Chamber Foundation, the research arm of the Chamber of Commerce.

As CTV News first reported, multiple sources have said trade discussions between the U.S. and Canada have restarted in earnest ahead of the midterm elections with the U.S. keen to make a deal.

  • EXCLUSIVE: Canada hasn’t yet closed door on U.S. trade deal ahead of midterms

Perry hopes it happens soon.

“We want to make sure that we’re able to build those relationships at supplier networks in nations across the world, and to continue to have that predictable operations so that we’re able to create more goods and services and create better jobs for Georgians.”

items.title: Nova Scotia Power CEO Vivek Sood departing after less than a year on the job
items.description: Nova Scotia Power Inc. CEO Vivek Sood is leaving his post at the province’s privately owned utility less than a year after taking its top job.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Nova Scotia Power CEO Vivek Sood is seen in the company's Halifax headquarters on Tuesday March 31, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Devin Stevens]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Devin Stevens</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Nova Scotia Power Inc. CEO Vivek Sood is leaving his post at the province’s privately owned utility less than a year after taking its top job.
items.body:
Nova Scotia Power Inc. CEO Vivek Sood is leaving his post at the province’s privately owned utility less than a year after taking its top job.

Sood, a former executive at grocer Sobeys and its parent firm Empire Company Ltd., was a Nova Scotia Power director before he became the Emera Inc. subsidiary’s chief executive in March 2026. The utility said in a news release Tuesday that Sood chose not to renew his contract.

In a social media post, Sood said he was proud to have restored stability after taking over during the fallout of a March 2025 cyberattack that saw the personal information of more than 370,000 customers accessed by what the utility has said it believes were Russia-based actors.

The attack spurred multiple investigations, disrupted billing systems for a year and caused many customers to complain about inflated bills much higher than usual. Sood said shortly after taking the job that rebuilding trust with customers was one of his top priorities.

“There is more work ahead, but I leave knowing Nova Scotia Power has a strong foundation and a talented team to carry it forward,” said Sood.

He said he can now spend more time on his board work with Halifax’s Saint Mary’s University and the Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21.

Nova Scotia Power said Chris Smith, its current executive vice-president of finance and commercial, will take over as permanent CEO on Nov. 2.

Smith is the former president of Nova Scotia natural gas distributor Eastward Energy and a chartered professional accountant. He first joined Nova Scotia Power in 2017, according to his company profile.

The utility declined interview requests for both executives Tuesday.

“Chris is a proven leader who deeply understands the business and the importance of maintaining focus on the priorities ahead,” Emera CEO Scott Balfour said in a statement.

“That includes supporting the new Nova Scotia Independent Energy System Operator through a complex transition in generation and system planning, while continuing Nova Scotia Power’s work to improve reliability and manage cost impacts for customers.”

  • Download the CTV News App for breaking news alerts and video on all the top stories

When Sood’s appointment was first announced in February 2026, Premier Tim Houston urged him to change course on a rate hike application that was then before regulators.

“While I wish the new CEO more success than his predecessors, I am concerned this announcement is less about real change and more about deflecting from a long-standing pattern of failure,” said Houston, also the provincial minister of energy, said in a lengthy social media post in February. Houston’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

Sood stickhandled the contentious power rate hearing to its conclusion, with a 3.1 per cent price hike going into effect in May 2026 and a 3.9 per cent increase set to hit power bills in January 2027.

He also oversaw the utility’s regulatory application to refinance nearly $1 billion worth of assets, including several coal plants scheduled to close by 2030.

If approved, the complicated financial scheme, known as “securitization” could result in a 2.9 per cent surcharge on residential power bills next year. Nova Scotia Power has said lower interest rates from securitization will save customers $265 million over 30 years compared with not using the finance mechanism.

Meanwhile, Nova Scotia Power’s Halifax-based parent firm Emera announced earlier this month plans to merge with Calgary’s Canadian Utilities to create a new company worth $72 billion and ranking among North America’s largest utilities.

The combined utility company will operate under the Emera banner, keeping its public company headquarters in Halifax and corporate and operational offices in Calgary and Edmonton. Post-merger Emera is to serve six million customers spanning various parts of Canada, as well as the United States, Mexico, the Caribbean and Australia.

items._ogDesc: Nova Scotia’s premier says the only company with rights to explore for offshore oil and gas in the province missed Monday’s deposit deadline.
items.body:
HALIFAX — Nova Scotia’s premier says the only company with rights to explore for offshore oil and gas in the province missed Monday’s deposit deadline.

Tim Houston said in a social media post Monday that Nova Scotia’s Inceptio Oil and Gas would not be able to put $50 million down as required.

In April, regulators approved a $210-million exploration bid from the company, led by Nova Scotian James Edens, who is also president of Scotland-based Inceptio UK.

Inceptio needed to put down 25 per cent of the bid price — about $52 million — in order to obtain a licence for activities such as seismic testing and drilling. Ottawa and the province had twice previously directed the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator to extend the deadline, in May and August.

Edens said in an email that the company was pleased with the support it received from the provincial and federal governments, including the extensions. He said there was significant interest in the project, but the company could not secure enough domestic investment in time to meet the deposit deadline.

“Foreign investment was sourced, but was limited by mandatory reviews for foreign ownership in natural resources, with incompatible timelines with our security-posting needs,” wrote Edens. “We will monitor the licensing framework proposed in future call for bids for supportive change.”

The regulator said in an email Tuesday that legislation requires an exploration licence to be issued within six months of the call for bids closing.

With the deadline passed, a new call for bids will have to be issued before Inceptio or any other company can seek to explore in Nova Scotia’s waters. Those calls are typically issued around mid-April.

Inceptio Ltd., which has common principal shareholders with Inceptio Oil and Gas but is a separate company, had previously been approved for an offshore exploration licence. However, the provincial and federal governments jointly vetoed the approval in 2023.

Jonathan Wilkinson, Natural Resources minister at the time, said the $1.5-million bid was small, raising questions around risk and complexity of the project.

Houston said in a social media post Monday that the lack of progress is a setback, but the province remains committed to developing its offshore resources.

“Hard things are hard but we will continue laying the groundwork for a stronger, more resilient Nova Scotia that can stand on its own and meet the challenges of tomorrow,” Houston said on social media.

The premier has pushed hard to kick-start Nova Scotia’s resource sector since his second term began in 2024. He has said the province needs to exploit its natural gas and other resources to better withstand economic challenges from the United States, including President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Along with a renewed focus on offshore oil and gas, his government has pursued wind and hydrogen development, and has lifted long-term bans on onshore natural gas fracking as well as uranium mining.

While the private sector has demonstrated interest in wind and hydrogen, there’s been little activity in Nova Scotia’s offshore fossil fuel sector since the Sable and Deep Panuke gas projects shut down in 2018. The projects combined to generate billions in royalties for the province over 25 years of offshore exploration and development.

There’s about 90-billion cubic metres of gas confirmed to exist on the Scotian shelf and a potential for more than 10 times that amount, says the province.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press

Correction

This is a corrected article. A previous version incorrectly stated that Inceptio Oil and Gas was based in the U.K. In fact, the company is incorporated in Nova Scotia. While Inceptio Oil and Gas has principal shareholders in common with Inceptio Ltd. and Inceptio UK Ltd., the companies do not have ownership stakes in each another.

The post Canadian Real Estate Correction Now Spreading To Other Provinces appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate prices fell in 8 of 9 provinces last month. Ontario and BC lead the 22.5% drop from peak, but the broader market is now sliding.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate correction has largely been concentrated in one province, but that may change soon. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell in September. All but one province moved lower, with BC going from resilient to leading the way lower in the past year. Other provinces, some of which hit record highs in 2026, are now making sharp moves lower. An anomaly or is the rest of the market ready to correct too?

Canadian Real Estate Prices Have Dropped $189k Since Peak

Before the provincial breakdown, let’s quickly review the national data. Canadian home prices fell 0.9% (-$5,700) to $651,400 in September, 3.4% (-$22,700) lower than last year and a whopping 22.5% (-$189,000) below peak. As previously noted, the lion’s share of that downward pressure is in Ontario—and to a lesser extent, BC. However, other provinces may be ready to join the correction.

Only One Province Saw Prices Climb, Nova Scotia Abruptly Plunges

Canadian real estate prices: Monthly change in dollars, September 2026.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Home prices only climbed in 1 of CREA’s 9 provincial indexes. The PEI benchmark rose 1.4% (+$5.1k), but that follows a 4.0% (-$15.6k) drop in August. Bucking the trend and rolling back part of the largest drop in PEI’s history are two very different stories.

The remaining 8 of 9 CREA indexes showed declines. The largest monthly decline was in Nova Scotia (-2.7%; -$11.8k), driven by an abrupt plunge in Halifax. A 1.3% (-$4.9k) drop in Saskatchewan and Ontario’s 1.0% (-$7.6k), round out the three biggest drops lower last month.

Despite the broad declines, most provinces remain higher than last year. These gains are mostly concentrated in Eastern Canada, while the Prairies were stable. Newfoundland’s 5.5% (+$18.6k) climb puts it in the lead for annual growth. It was followed by Saskatchewan, which came in 2.8% (+$10.4k) higher than last year, and New Brunswick at 2.7% (+$9.1k).

Leading the way lower over the past year is BC, where September came in 4.7% (-$42.4k) lower than last year. Ontario followed with a 3.9% (-$29.6k) drop over the same period, followed by Nova Scotia, whose monthly plunge pushed prices 2.5% (-$11.0k) lower.

Canada’s Real Estate Correction Has Only Hit 2 Provinces So Far

Decline in home prices from peak, by province.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Not one province remains at peak, though Newfoundland is only 1.0% (-$3.7k) below its July 2026 record high. Despite peaking in the same month, PEI has plunged more than double at 2.7% (-$10.5k). Neither province is that far from the peak, and all but two provinces remain close to the record highs.

Ontario is one of those two, plunging 26.7% (-$268.8k) since its March 2022 peak. BC is a distant second, down 16.7% (-$174.3k). That massive 10-point gap highlights just how concentrated this “crash” actually is. Nova Scotia sits in third at just 4.1% (-$18.2k) below its peak. But remember, BC’s decline was in the single-digits until well into last year. Nova Scotia’s abrupt monthly plunge could mean a broader correction is just getting started.

Whether Canada’s housing slump has another leg lower is anyone’s guess. The national index is down 22.5% from peak, but only Ontario has seen a drop larger than that. It’s being called a historic, 4-year market correction—yet most provinces are still hugging their record highs. Ultimately, corrections occur to resolve market inefficiencies for buyers, not just a national model. Until regional markets make sense to local buyers, activity will remain tame.

items.title: Why AI can’t replace mortgage brokers
items.description: REMIC CEO says brokers aren’t going anywhere even amid the rise of artificial intelligence in the mortgage process
items.content: <p>REMIC CEO says brokers aren’t going anywhere even amid the rise of artificial intelligence in the mortgage process</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639287227579783949.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: REMIC CEO says brokers aren’t going anywhere even amid the rise of artificial intelligence in the mortgage process
items.body:
Joe White, founder and CEO of REMIC, joins us to talk about how mortgage agents and brokers should approach AI, and why the profession’s value is clearer than ever. Joe explains the risk of AI tools that sound completely confident but get the fine details wrong, and why “gating” AI, so it only draws on accurate information, matters in an industry where clients are making the biggest purchase of their lives.

[00:00] Ask them, have you run anything by AI and what did it tell you? Yeah, it's the wild west out there right now. The fact is that brokers are licensed, AI isn't. So, it treats us like kids, telling us what we want to hear confidently. If you don't adopt it, you're going to be left behind.

[00:28] Fergal McAlinden: All right. So, next up we have got Dwight Funding and Chief Executive Officer of REMIC. For you with REMIC, what are some of the main conversations that you're hoping to have today and who are the main people you want to get in front of?

[00:40] Joe White: Yeah, for us it's important, I think, that industry understands the next steps of evolution in their career. So, you started as mortgage agent level one, then you go to level two, then you become a broker. And all the while you're going through that, it's necessary to learn how to use AI and social media, which is another program that we offer. So, we're here just letting people know that wherever you're at in your career, we have something that we think will be of benefit to you.

[01:12] Fergal McAlinden: And you're saying that to chart the rise of AI over the past few years, we've always known that technology and social media and all of that have been big game changers for the industry. AI has almost turbocharged it. What do brokers and agents have to keep in mind? What's been the biggest changes for you or what are the main things that agents and brokers need to keep in mind about the rise of AI?

[01:30] Joe White: Oh, that's a great question. I think the main thing, and what I'm going to be speaking about on the stage this afternoon, is gating the AI and checking it. AI has a wonderful ability to give you an answer that sounds incredibly confident with, but in many cases it's the fine details that it gets wrong.

[01:53] Because it's trained on everything out there on the internet and that means that it's trained on wrong information as well as right information. So, when we talk about gating the AI, that's basically enclosing it in like a pen where it just has access to accurate information. It doesn't go out and get inaccurate information, which is a big problem right now.

[02:17] Fergal McAlinden: Especially when we talk about the mortgage industry where people are making the biggest purchase of their lives. We've all seen what ChatGPT does when it confidently says something that's not the case at all. It's something that not a lot of people would trust exclusively to AI when they're making a home purchase.

[02:33] Joe White: Yeah, a lot of people are using AI for their home purchase. And when they do a search online, especially on Google, they don't realize that they're talking to AI when Gemini is giving them a summary. That's a problem because everything is so confident. All of these AI systems are so confident.

[02:56] So, one of the strategies we talk about is when you're taking a new client, ask them, "Have you run anything by AI and what did it tell you?" Because I think one of the most important things for brokers and agents to do now is correct the wrong information that people are getting from AI. It's the wild west out there right now.

[03:16] Fergal McAlinden: Absolutely. And it kind of shines a light as well on the value of brokers, too. There were a lot of existential questions about what was going to happen to the mortgage agent or broker profession as AI continued to rise. But what you mentioned is kind of proof that the profession isn't going anywhere despite this.

[03:32] Joe White: Oh, 100%. The fact is that brokers are licensed, AI isn't. The fact that brokers have errors and omissions insurance, so if something goes wrong, the client's protected. AI can't do that.

[03:47] What consumers, I think, will understand over time is that what they get with dealing with a broker is competency. It takes years to create. Confidence, you know, I talk to my kids and I tell them something confidently just because I want them to do something. And I don't know if what I'm saying is true or not, but I use it confidently. That's what AI does. It treats us like kids, telling us what we want to hear confidently. And at the end of the day, I think the broker's value is their competence. And that takes years to establish.

[04:18] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And then obviously there's the question of what happens whenever something goes wrong or there's an issue. And that human touch really comes in as well with brokers and how they can deal with their clients, which AI might not be able to do.

[04:31] Joe White: Yeah, absolutely. You're dealing with somebody who's under a power of sale or can't close on a condo. They need some empathy. They need somebody that can understand.

[04:43] In addition to that, it's necessary for consumers to know that brokers have an entire regulatory body behind them. And that regulatory body helps ensure that consumers are getting accurate information. That doesn't happen in AI. There's nobody there ensuring it. And the regulators don't have the ability to regulate the AI like they do individuals.

[05:09] So, I think over time it's going to become much clearer that it's vitally important for consumers to use somebody who has that backdrop of a license and a regulatory environment.

[05:20] Fergal McAlinden: Is that a shortfall, maybe a danger point for the industry at the minute, the fact that there aren't those regulatory stop gaps when it comes to AI and on the advice that is coming?

[05:31] Joe White: Yeah, I think it is. I spoke to an MPP recently and brought that to their attention, that AI is giving confidently wrong answers and acting like a mortgage broker. I asked ChatGPT, "I need a mortgage. Can you act like a mortgage broker?" "Sure, I can do that. Here are all the questions that I'm going to ask you and all the information that I need."

[05:58] And now it's asking me for financial information. But the problem is, I think, in the regulatory environment, they're not sure how to regulate it. Who would oversee the regulation of AI when it comes to financial services?

[06:14] I understand that there is legislation that generally covers third-party advice, but it's not enough. Somebody goes online this morning and starts typing in and has a 15-minute conversation with Claude or ChatGPT or DeepSeek, and they walk out of there thinking, "Now I know what I have to do." And they don't know. They could be wrong.

[06:29] Fergal McAlinden: Sure. And there's an element of AI tools as well. I find that it's almost anxious to reassure people. Maybe it takes your side a little bit more than a broker who gives kind of hard-headed advice or the right information would necessarily do. So, maybe with AI tools you're not necessarily getting what's always best for you.

[06:46] Joe White: 100%. And I think it goes back to the entire OpenAI, Anthropic. Their goal is to have an AI that gives you information that you find valuable and helpful, but it's wanting to please you by giving you information that makes you happy.

[07:02] Whereas a broker's job is to give you information that's grounded in reality. So, an AI might end up telling you, "Yeah, yeah, you can do this and you can get approved. So, go start looking for a house." Whereas a broker might have a more realistic outlook on that.

[07:20] Fergal McAlinden: Absolutely. Okay, well, Joe, great to talk to you today. Anything else that you want brokers to keep in mind before we let you go or any other conversations that you're going to be having with them today?

[07:29] Joe White: Yeah, I think the one thing to remember is AI, although it has its shortcomings, it's here to stay and you have to adopt it. While others are adopting it, if you don't adopt it, you're going to be left behind. But you have to do it in a very intelligent, meaningful, intentional way. And that's what we're going to be talking about.

[07:50] Fergal McAlinden: And just a word, Joe, on the event itself. What's your perspective on how it's gone so far? We've had mortgage summits in the past which you'd been involved with. This is the first time as a Mortgage Fest. How's it been for you so far?

[08:02] Joe White: Yeah, it's great. It's a really nice environment. People seem to be enjoying themselves. I'm enjoying myself and checking out the different speakers as well.

[08:12] Fergal McAlinden: Brad Stuffle, we're looking forward to your presentation later on. We'll see you here next year.

[08:15] Joe White: Thank you very much.

items.title: Mortgage market ‘still recovering’ from BoC’s COVID rate cuts, says lender president
items.description: The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive
items.content: <p>The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287200172090755.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is gearing up for what many pundits say could be the start of a new rate-hiking cycle – but the housing and mortgage markets are still dealing with the impact of its COVID-era rate policy even years later, according to the president of a prominent mortgage lender.

The central bank slashed its benchmark rate to a rock-bottom 0.25% at the onset of the pandemic, helping cause a homebuying frenzy as mortgage rates plunged and borrowers jumped into the market.

A series of rapid rate hikes in 2022 and 2023 put a halt to that housing boom, but Westboro Mortgage Investment Corporation president Derek Serra (pictured top) told Canadian Mortgage Professional he still sees the negative effects of the low-rate era seeping through.

“I think that we’re still kind of recovering from the decision to have lowered interest rates during COVID. And the outcome of that decision sparked such an incredible inflationary time for Canadians,” he said. “I’ve been in banking for 30 years, and I’ve always seen Canadians using the equity in their home as an opportunity for them to pay for their kids’ education.

“There was almost a kind of a familiarity or a consistency with expecting a little bit of growth in the value of your home. And so when these inflationary times came through COVID, which was triggered by the very low interest rates, the average Canadian saw rapid increases in their property values – which at the time sparked them to do more than what they usually do without, necessarily, the kind of long-term perspective.”

‘There was the opinion that rates… would stay low for a long time’

In 2025 and 2026, scores of mortgages originated during the pandemic have come up for renewal, almost always at much higher rates compared with five years prior.

That trend is part of the reason mortgage delinquencies are climbing, with Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) indicating on Tuesday it doesn’t expect the rise of mortgage arrears in Ontario to end until the middle of next year.

Serra suggested the Bank of Canada’s decision to dramatically cut rates in 2020 might have been the wrong one looking back.

“There was also kind of the opinion that rates would be low and stay low for a long time, and obviously that shifted for a variety of reasons,” he said. “And now we’re seeing the outcome of that decision.

“In hindsight, it’s always easy to look back and question, but you wonder if maybe we hadn’t dropped rates at the time, we would have felt more pain then – but it would have been a different kind of 2026 now.”

As the central bank embarked on a rate-hiking spree in 2022 and 2023, industry and expert opinion was divided on whether governor Tiff Macklem had misled Canadians by suggesting that interest rates wouldn’t be rising anytime soon.

Macklem told the House of Commons standing committee on finance in November 2020 that Canadians “can be confident that borrowing costs are going to remain very low for a very long time” – but within less than three years, the BoC’s benchmark rate had shot up by 475 basis points.

Critics said that reassurance may have convinced Canadians the time was right to purchase a home without factoring in higher costs down the line. Macklem’s defenders, on the other hand, pointed to unexpected developments including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the further supply chain snarls caused by the emergence of the Omicron COVID variant.

Appraisal challenges continue in higher-rate environment

As well as causing challenges for borrowers at renewal time, the post-pandemic march toward higher rates poured cold water on a red-hot housing market. In that environment, appraisal challenges have arisen because there are so few transactions in many cities to judge whether or how far a property’s value may have fallen.

Serra, though, pointed to some recent cause for optimism on that front. “The good news is we’ve seen a little bit of increase in the past four weeks in purchase transactions, and that is a really good sign,” he said.

“It’s an early indicator… but as we see purchase transactions, even if they’re at lower values, we’re able to now properly assess where the market’s at. If you’re living in a community where there haven’t been any sales, it’s very difficult to substantiate the value of these properties, especially for clients who are looking for higher loan-to-values.”

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Amber Bracken]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">AMBER BRACKEN</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and the United Conservatives are back in the legislature for the first time since the separation referendum, and Smith is dismissing suggestions it was a waste.
items.body:
EDMONTON — Alberta politicians returned to the legislature Tuesday for the first time since the separation referendum – and Premier Danielle Smith told the chamber she has no regrets holding the vote.

“We should never regret democracy,” Smith said in question period.

The vote result, she said, sent a clear message.

She was responding to Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi, who asked her if she regretted putting Albertans through the exercise and pitting them against each other.

Last week, three-quarters of Alberta voters chose in a provincewide referendum to stay in Canada rather than hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

Smith said Tuesday she was grateful for those who voted with her on keeping Alberta in Canada and repeated that it was the side she had campaigned on. That last comment drew laughs from the NDP benches.

Smith has said she had to call the vote to quell a distracting debate in Alberta, but critics say Smith was simply catering to separatists in her United Conservative Party to prevent them from turning against her.

Smith has already faced pushback. A few United Conservative constituency associations have called for a leadership review.

Earlier Tuesday, UCP backbencher Scott Cyr announced that, to his dismay, his Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul constituency association passed a motion a day earlier calling for a leadership review.

Cyr, in a social media post, said it passed narrowly — 10 votes to nine — in a secret ballot. He said he doesn’t agree with the outcome and that it’s time to rally behind Smith’s leadership.

“With the 2027 provincial election approaching, I am concerned about the consequences of continued internal division within the United Conservative Party,” he wrote.

Other UCP constituency associations have voted to show support for Smith. The party’s annual general meeting in Calgary is one month away.

Mitch Sylvestre, president of Cyr’s constituency association, is a prominent face in Alberta’s separatist movement.

Sylvestre and others behind the independence push have set their sights on ousting Smith as party leader over her support for keeping Alberta in Canada.

Smith is seeking to rein in separatist elements in her party ahead of the next election, set for Oct. 18, 2027.

She said last week that the referendum result wasn’t just a mandate for the government but a mandate for her UCP. She encouraged separatist leaders within the UCP to turn the page or find a new party to join. She said that directive also applies to future candidates or party officials, including constituency association board members.

Sylvestre responded by saying he won’t be leaving.

The UCP also lost a legislature member heading into Tuesday.

Backbencher Shane Getson announced Monday he was quitting politics completely and immediately, citing unspecified personal reasons.

Smith’s party now has 46 seats in the legislature. The NDP has 39, and there is one Progressive Tory.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

items.title: Costly Construction, Decades Of Delays: Canada’s Project Leaders Get A New Playbook
items.description:
For much of the past two decades, Canada approached major projects with a simple idea: write the contract well enough, and the project would essentially look after itself. Each risk sat with a party ready to handle it, so when something went wrong, everyone knew who to turn to.

But it hasn’t worked out that way. Canada is one of the most expensive places in the world to build, and paying top dollar still doesn’t keep projects from running late (and over budget). That’s a problem at any time, but an even bigger one today, with the transportation, water, energy, natural resource, military and information technology projects currently being planned carrying multi-billion-dollar price tags — not to mention stakes in trade, sovereignty, national unity, and climate change. For developers and city-builders, these are the projects that determine where and how growth happens.

“What we’ve learned, in the last five to 10 years in particular, is that the contract is not going to save everything,” says Matti Siemiatycki, Professor of Geography and Planning, and Director of the University of Toronto’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities. “We’ve realized that contracting is really a relational business, and that the relational skills amongst the parties who are delivering the projects are central to their success.”

The reliance on contracts has roots. In the early 2000s, public-private partnerships, or P3s, became the default for major projects, and by Siemiatycki’s account, most jurisdictions set up dedicated P3 agencies (many required the model outright). He assures that P3s do have their place. They just don’t suit every project, but the industry tried to apply them to nearly everything.

This history leaves many of today’s senior project leaders in a challenging position. They came up during the P3 era with “excellent project management skills,” Siemiatycki says, “but they were trained in a world that was very adversarial.”

The Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy was built to help those leaders move from contract-first thinking to the relationship-driven work major projects now demand. Launched by U of T’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities and the Rotman School of Management, it’s the only executive program built specifically for major project leaders in Canada. It’s designed for public and private sector leaders with 10 to 15 years of experience who are preparing to take on the largest projects in their organizations.

These industry players already know how to run a project, so the curriculum builds on that experience, with a heavy focus on leading one: building teams when several organizations share a project, understanding infrastructure as a system, rather than a linear Gantt chart, and recognizing the biases that lead projects to underestimate costs and overestimate benefits. Negotiation and conflict resolution get dedicated focus as well, “because so many of these projects end up in some form of litigation or conflict,” Siemiatycki says. Rotman’s Geoffrey Leonardelli, Professor of Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management, brings the school’s executive leadership expertise to the faculty.

Over six months, the hybrid program combines three three-day in-person modules at Rotman in Toronto with monthly live online sessions, mentorship, a capstone project, and the chance to work through a real issue from participants’ own professional contexts.

Graduates earn a certificate from the Rotman School of Management.

Applications are open now for the inaugural cohort, which launches April 13, 2027. Siemiatycki and his team are reviewing applications as they come in, with the goal of building an intentionally diverse cohort of leaders from civil infrastructure, energy, natural resources, and industrial projects.

The program’s model has a track record abroad; the United Kingdom and Australia both run similar academies. The Canadian version is distinct, though, in that it’s shaped to suit how projects actually get built here. “If you don’t understand our culture and you don’t understand how we collaborate, the projects ultimately end up in miscommunication, and things going wrong,” Siemiatycki says. “Having the program be by Canadians, for Canadians is really important.”

When that collaboration breaks down, the companies at the table feel it. “The risk is borne by the company, especially for construction,” Siemiatycki explains. “And if it goes badly, they’re going to wear it.”

Further, the academy puts public and private sector leaders in the same room on purpose. Over six months, each side learns how the other thinks about a project, and both leave with a network to call on, if and when something goes sideways.

“Ultimately we’ll build a cohort of people that can deliver for Canada,” Siemiatycki says.

The first cohort is where that network begins. Looking forward, the plan is to grow the academy into a national program delivered locally across the country, with each new cohort adding leaders who know how to work across the public and private sides of a project. Many of the organizations Siemiatycki has spoken with already see their participation as an investment in the sector, as well as in their own teams.

As that network grows, more of the country’s major projects can be led by people who already understand how their counterparts think, and who know who to call when things get difficult. It’s the relational side of delivery Siemiatycki says the contract was never going to cover on its own.

Applications for the inaugural cohort are open now, and organizations ready to add their people to that network can nominate a member of their team to apply. Applications submitted by November 30 receive 20% off tuition.

items.title: Some Canadian homebuyers tune out tariff noise as trade war rumbles on
items.description: Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty
items.content: <p>Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286291616924369.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty
items.body:
Geopolitical chaos and global economic uncertainty have stretched into 2026, pushing a hoped-for Canadian housing market recovery even further down the line as potential homebuyers wait for a calmer environment to emerge before making their move.

Bond market unease has sent five-year Government of Canada yields higher in recent months, pushing fixed mortgage rates upwards, while speculation is growing about at least one potential Bank of Canada rate hike in the months ahead.

Would-be buyers are still keeping a close eye on the latest political news – but while the announcement of US tariffs at the beginning of last year sent shockwaves around bond markets and hugely dented homebuyer confidence, a degree of acceptance has set in among mortgage shoppers about the trade war.

That’s according to Ottawa-based Smart Debt Mortgages broker Chris Allard (pictured top), who told Canadian Mortgage Professional many clients were still determined to push ahead with their purchase plans even with no end to the trade dispute in sight.

“I get the perception that people have largely tried to tune out some of the news and keep a positive mindset,” he said. “But there’s no doubt that everyone’s aware of what’s happening, and they’re aware that rates are rising and there’s significant concern for that.

“Now, the commentary that I often hear from borrowers, and this is true, is we see when Trump speaks now, the markets don’t automatically go up or automatically go down right away. And so that translates into the conversation that we’re having with our clients because they’re now recognizing that maybe it’s just a bunch of noise.”

Borrowers are still cognizant of the impact a big, unexpected development in the trade war would have for the economy and their plans – but they’re equally focused on making their mortgage work and optimizing their financial picture to move forward with their deal, Allard said.

“They’re trying to just look at their personal budget and try to make an educated decision based on the current environment rather than predicting if home values are up or down or rates are up or down,” he said. “They’re going, ‘What are my payments now? Am I comfortable now? And do I have a safety net?’”

BoC rate not expected to surge, even if a hike is on the way

Opinion is divided among leading economists on what’s in store from the Bank of Canada’s decision this Wednesday. Experts including Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge don’t see a hike on the way yet, although Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) now marginally expects a 25-basis-point jump.

Most of the country’s top banks expect rate hikes to arrive at some point over the next year – but none are predicting the Bank of Canada’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable mortgage rates, will hit the highs seen in 2023-24.

That’s welcome news for borrowers, according to Allard. “I think a lot of Canadians might be surprised that the banks are not projecting significant prime rate increases,” he said. “It turns out that we did see fixed rate increases – and now it looks as though there won’t be significant prime rate increases.

“So I believe that just means that we might have more clients going into variable once they start to understand that dynamic.”

Clients focus on variable amid fixed-rate rises

Allard said he’s recently noted an increase in clientele wanting variable rates with a static payment amid a wider move away from fixed rates. “Bank of Montreal [BMO] offers that, TD Bank offers that, there’s a few others that offer it,” he said.

“Borrowers are [saying] ‘Well, maybe I can benefit from a rate in the high threes, have a stable payment, even though I’m taking a variable-rate product.’ It’s a really interesting move that we’re seeing from a consumer behaviour standpoint.”

items.title: BoC preview: What to expect from Wednesday's huge decision
items.description: Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move
items.content: <p>Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286370231956432.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move
items.body:
The Bank of Canada’s penultimate interest rate decision of 2026 arrives on Wednesday (October 28), and there's no consensus among experts on whether a rate hold or hike is in store.

The central bank has kept rates unchanged for nearly 12 months, with its last move in either direction arriving almost a year to the day of Wednesday’s announcement – a 25-basis-point cut on October 29, 2025.

The BoC’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable mortgage rates in Canada, has held steady since then as decisionmakers adopted a cautious approach during tense times marked by global economic uncertainty, a worsening trade dispute with the US, and inflation fears sparked by the US-Iran war.

Is a hike in store on Wednesday?

The Bank is at an “inflection point” as its next decision looms, according to Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) Economics, whose economists now say a quarter-point hike is the likeliest outcome from Wednesday’s meeting.

Still, that’s by no means a surefire thing. RBC’s Frances Donald (chief economist) and Nathan Janzen (assistant chief economist) see an almost equal probability that the BoC will hold steady this month but signal a rate hike on the way in December or January.

 Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge, meanwhile, doesn’t expect a hike between now and the end of the year – but said he anticipates the BoC will begin raising interest rates at some point in 2027, potentially in the spring.

But 19 of 34 economists polled by Reuters last week see a central bank rate jump to 2.50% on Wednesday, with a majority also pencilling in a further increase before March.

The main reason for the sudden prospect of a rate hike is concern about the national inflation outlook. The consumer price index (CPI) ticked higher last month, hitting 3.1% as surging fuel prices pushed prices higher.

However, observers including National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéfane Marion believe that increase was milder than might have been expected – strengthening the case for a further rate hold.

“Core inflation is still at 2%,” Marion said during an address at last week’s Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary. “I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking [on October 28] and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive.”

What the BoC decision will mean for mortgages

If the Bank increases rates on Wednesday, variable mortgage rates would also move higher because banks typically raise their prime rate in line with BoC moves.

Much attention will focus on the language used by BoC governor Tiff Macklem in his press conference after the announcement, with financial markets keeping a close eye on whether Macklem indicates rate increases are likely in the coming months.

As for the possible impact on the housing market of Wednesday’s decision?

A rate hold probably wouldn’t move the needle for national homebuying, which has remained sluggish through 2026 because of economic uncertainty and rising rates.

It’s unclear whether a rate hike would slow the market further, although activity has remained moribund as potential buyers stay on the sidelines even with rate increases on the horizon.

“You’d expect with lots of chatter about rate increases in Canada online bubbling through communities – plus the recent significant rise in fixed-rate mortgages in the United States – that there’d be some pull-ahead in activity,” Royal LePage president and chief executive officer Phil Soper told CMP earlier this month.

“You’d see some people that were planning to get into the market in the spring of 2027, for example, jumping in now to get ahead of anticipated higher borrowing costs. Yet we’re not seeing material changes in the trajectory of transaction volumes. It’s very flat.”

items.title: Calgary's industrial market sees strongest quarterly performance since 2022
items.description: Tight supply and rising rents could boost deal flow for commercial lenders and brokers
items.content: <p>Tight supply and rising rents could boost deal flow for commercial lenders and brokers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0356_639286894738396309.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tight supply and rising rents could boost deal flow for commercial lenders and brokers
items.body:
Calgary’s industrial market tightened sharply in the third quarter, with vacancy falling to its lowest level in three years, according to a new Avison Young report.

Net absorption, the net amount of space taken up by tenants, reached 3.6 million sq. ft. That was the strongest quarterly result since Q3 2022. Total vacancy fell to 2.9%, down 1.2 percentage points from the previous quarter and down from 4.7% a year earlier.

“Robust tenant demand absorbed most newly delivered space while also reducing existing vacancies,” the report said.

Supply stays tight

The availability rate, which includes space that is vacant or will soon be, dropped to 3.5%. Sublease space is limited at 0.6%, and the report said rents are firming as competition for quality space grows.

Developers have 3.8 million sq. ft. under construction across 16 projects. About 2.0 million sq. ft., or 52%, is already preleased. Only 1.4 million sq. ft. has been delivered so far in 2026, well below the five-year average of roughly 4.3 million sq. ft.

Large-bay space is especially scarce, and the report said large-format users may need to consider design-build solutions. It also cited a shortage of development-ready, serviced industrial land, particularly within city limits.

Vacancy fell in every submarket from a year earlier. Rocky View County/Balzac saw the biggest improvement, dropping from 12.2% to 4.5%. That submarket also holds more than half of the construction pipeline, at 2.1 million sq. ft.

Capital follows demand

Industrial building investment totalled $220 million in the quarter, according to figures from The Network. That brings the year-to-date total to $861 million, about 10% above the $785 million transacted in the same period of 2025.

Among the quarter’s notable deals, Dream Industrial bought a 159,650-sq.-ft. Southeast building for $31.25 million, or $196 per sq. ft. Avison Young also brokered new direct leases of 498,000, 486,000 and 365,000 sq. ft.

Other brokerages see a similar trend, though their numbers differ because methods vary. CBRE reported 3.8 million sq. ft. of absorption and a 3.6% availability rate. It also found owner-user sale options fell 27.7% to 65. Altus Group put Calgary’s availability at 4.9%, down 140 basis points from a year earlier. It put national availability at 6.2%.

What it means for borrowers and lenders

The Avison Young report listed rising rents, normalized borrowing costs and improved liquidity among the factors strengthening development spreads. It named macroeconomic uncertainty, inflation and elevated construction costs as headwinds.

Rates remain a variable. The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% on Sept. 2. It said upside inflation risks had increased and long-term bond yields had moved higher. Its next decision is scheduled for Oct. 28.

For brokers with industrial owner-user, investor or developer clients, the data points to a market where limited options and firmer rents may affect timing and financing. The report advised tenants with upcoming lease expiries or expansion plans to start their search early.

items.title: Housing and health funding cliffs loom as federal budget nears: RBC
items.description: Federal housing funding is projected to fall from more than $10 billion to $4 billion by 2028-29
items.content: <p>Federal housing funding is projected to fall from more than $10 billion to $4 billion by 2028-29</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0356_639286892527825539.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Federal housing funding is projected to fall from more than $10 billion to $4 billion by 2028-29
items.body:
Federal housing and health funding arrangements are set to wind down in 2027-28. The coming budget could signal how Ottawa plans to replace them, according to RBC Economics.

Finance minister François-Philippe Champagne will table Budget 2026 on Nov. 5. RBC assistant chief economist Cynthia Leach said in an Oct. 26 analysis that the budget’s task is “less about new programs and more about disciplined execution.”

“Even with immediate pressures contained, two spending areas must soon be accommodated,” Leach wrote.

Housing money set to shrink

Budget 2026 could release the next version of the National Housing Strategy, which winds down in 2027-28, RBC said.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) has highlighted that federal housing funding drops from more than $10 billion in 2026-27 to $4 billion by 2028-29, even with Build Canada Homes. Recent measures, such as development charge reforms, may have lifted that profile, but they appear temporary, RBC said.

Build Canada Homes launched with $13 billion in initial funding. The PBO projects it will produce about 26,000 units and has said it is expected to add only a modest amount to housing supply. In March, Finance Canada described its full suite of housing programs as totalling roughly $40 billion.

RBC said Ottawa has responded to affordability pressures with tariff and oil-shock support for vulnerable households. It described the economy as slowly improving, with housing “sideways” in many markets.

Health transfers also expire

Several provincial health funding arrangements end in 2027-28, RBC said. They include the 5% guaranteed Canada Health Transfer escalator and one-off agreements worth about $3 billion or more a year.

Provinces are increasingly calling for a permanently higher federal share, as rising health-care costs drove deteriorating 2026 budgets, the analysis said. After a recent one-year extension of mental health funding, health minister Marjorie Michel has designated the broader issue as one for 2027.

On both files, Leach said RBC will look for efficiencies and clear, lasting terms.

“We’ll be looking for Ottawa to push for efficiencies … and for eventual agreements ideally to delineate long-term commitments rather than funding patches that punt the issue,” she wrote.

Tight fiscal room

RBC estimates $57 billion in new five-year spending commitments since the spring update, led by the $36 billion corporate tax mega deduction. It said deficits could run more than $15 billion deeper by 2030-31 than the spring update projected.

The PBO now expects a $63.3 billion deficit in 2026-27 and a balanced operating budget by 2028-29, a year later than the government promised, the Canadian Press reported. The finance minister’s spokesperson said the PBO’s assumptions differ from the government’s.

Rates add pressure. RBC noted the 10-year Government of Canada bond yield is up 40 basis points over four months. The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% in September and is scheduled to announce its next decision Oct. 28.

For brokers who work with builders, investors and affordable-rental clients, the funding timeline will affect how much federal support is available in coming years. RBC said it does not expect new funding for those areas in this budget, but it will watch how Ottawa frames the path ahead.
