The post Canadian Real Estate Needs More Immigration, Foreign Buyers: National Bank appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: National Bank warns Canada’s housing market needs higher immigration and foreign buyers to clear a record inventory of unsold homes and avoid a demographic cliff.
items.body:
Canadian real estate remains out of reach for young adults, but the show must go on. That’s the takeaway from a new housing report from National Bank of Canada. Slow home sales have led to a backlog of developer inventory, but billions in public bailouts are being used to support prices. National Bank urges policymakers to increase their immigration targets and reintroduce foreign buyers to help developers reduce inventory.

Canadian Real Estate In A Slump Despite Billions In Bailouts

The Great Canadian Real Estate Slump isn’t exactly news, but not everyone may be aware of how slow it’s been. Over 1 in 4 (28%) newly completed homes remain unsold, charting new territory for excess supply. “The inventory of completed and unsold housing units across all census metropolitan areas stands at 20,700 units, its highest level since records began in 1990,” warns the bank.

Existing homes aren’t doing much better. Seasonally adjusted sales saw a monthly drop of 2.3% in September, sliding 13% below the 10-year average. While Canadian home prices are now in the biggest correction on record, the almost 5-year slump only rolled back 13 months of price gains. That’s with taxpayer-backed bailouts.

“This demonstrates that the market is so weak that it requires public support,” writes National Bank.

Policymakers aren’t dabbling in support either—they’re fully immersed in the practice. The bank cites Ontario’s $1.3 billion bailout to help investors buy 2,200 unsold Toronto condos. They also cite Ottawa and British Columbia’s $1.45 billion program for roughly the same number of condos. These programs are massive, but even taxpayer-funded bulk buying isn’t enough to clear the backlog.

The bank urges policymakers to drum up more demand. Not from the young adults struggling with shelter costs. They can’t afford to buy a home. They’re calling on Ottawa to look beyond its borders to support prices. Seriously.

Big Six Bank Calls For Higher Immigration To Improve Demand

Canadian real estate prices surged from 2020 and finally peaked in March 2022. That occurred during the pandemic’s population slump, when population growth plummeted to near historic lows. Canada ramped up immigration to unprecedented levels as the slump kicked off. Despite a timing mismatch, reduced immigration is often cited as extending the downturn. The narrative was reinforced by StatCan’s population estimates that revealed a historic contraction. However, that contraction also didn’t happen.

The agency’s recent revisions show the 0.5% y/y decline reported at the start of 2026 was actually 0.5% growth. Ottawa’s plan to reduce non-permanent residents (NPR) to 5% of the population by 2027 is also unlikely. Not only did policymakers delay the target by a year, but NPRs currently represent 6.7% of the population. Canada needs to lose roughly 750,000 NPRs by the end of next year to make those numbers work. Still, the Big Six Bank is concerned.

Reducing NPRs to 5% of the total population will slow total growth to 0.2% in 2027 and 0.1% in 2028, notes the bank. They warn that sticking to the target will mean more downward pressure on housing. “In that context, we believe Ottawa should recalibrate its immigration policy through a targeted and gradual increase in immigration levels,” says National Bank.

Canadians Can’t Afford Homes? Sell Them To Foreign Investors

Canada’s foreign homebuyer restrictions are set to expire in a few months. “The ban on foreign home purchases, which expires on January 1, 2027, should not be extended but rather replaced by a more flexible policy,” explains National Bank.

Whether Canada will renew the moratorium is unclear, but policymakers aren’t fond of the measures. They began to quietly ease foreign buyer restrictions just 86 days after boasting of passing the ban. Canada has since elected Prime Minister Mark Carney, and while he hasn’t addressed the ban directly, the bank notes he recently laid the groundwork for a “controlled increase” in the population.

One of his key fundraisers in BC has been a little more vocal about foreign capital returning to housing. Shortly after PM Carney was elected, Vancouver’s “condo king” said he was working with the PM to drum up foreign capital for rentals.

National Bank sees foreign buyers as one of the only ways developers can sell the homes they built. “We believe it should not be renewed in its current form and that a more flexible model—such as Australia’s, which notably allows foreign buyers to purchase new homes—would help reduce the inventory of unsold housing,” argues the bank.

The bank’s take seems tone-deaf, but the implications are more disturbing. RBC recently found the average first-time buyer plans to buy at 41, 12 years later than current owners did. Separately, they found parents are increasingly helping their adult kids pay bills—a trend most parents attribute to a soaring cost of living rather than poor money management.

Canada’s young adults have been locked out of the housing market. For years they were told that more supply would close the gap, and building more would finally bring prices down. After taxpayers footed the bill to accelerate construction, the narrative abruptly shifted: prices can’t fall further because developers can’t make the math work. Since young adults can’t afford these prices, we suddenly need more temporary residents to support attractive rents that developers can pitch to foreign landlords.

items.body:
How much should governments pay to acquire land?

Under the BC NDP, the province has acquired several private properties for public use, paying what some industry sources describe as an unusual premium.

In fall 2025, the province announced that it had allocated $26 million to the Conseil scolaire francophone de la Colombie-Britannique to acquire 3044 Pratt St., Abbotsford, for a Francophone school. Provincial transaction data records a purchase price from a subsidiary of Abbotsford’s Azure Properties Group of $24.6 million, or $2 million an acre (leaving $1.4 million to cover transaction and closing costs).

On Jan. 29, the province acquired a 40-acre property at 1320 McKenzie Rd., Abbotsford, from a subsidiary of Richmond’s Panatch Group for $27.8 million, or $695,000 an acre. The property was used to grow vegetables, but Infrastructure BC plans to build a new Plant and Animal Health Centre on the site in partnership with the B.C. Ministry of Agriculture and Food.

On March 31, Crown corporation BC Hydro acquired a 21.75-acre parcel of vacant industrial land at 2161 Caribou Drive, Langford, from Vancouver-based developers Strand and Bastion Development Corp. for $52.5 million, or an average of $2.4 million an acre.

Howard Chai, who broke news of the deal at The Realist, noted that the “very specific” real estate needs of public entities often result in them appearing to pay more for sites than what other, less constrained parties might.

In the case of the school site in Abbotsford, industry sources indicate that the price was well above not just the $9.8 million value the BC Assessment assigned it on July 1, 2025, but also previous offers by private developers.

One well-known Vancouver developer who spoke to Western Investor on condition of anonymity, considered acquiring the property after it returned to market in fall 2022. Plans filed with the city at the time called for 130 townhomes on a developable area of seven acres. Pricing guidance stood at $24 million.

However, the site’s challenging topography, marked by steep slopes and fish-bearing streams, left just 3.5 acres suitable for development in the view of the developer. It couldn’t justify a price greater than $10 million.

An accepted offer in the range of $18 million ultimately came through, but during the due diligence process the purchaser reduced the offer to $15.5 million—again, because of site considerations. The deal collapsed.

An industry source familiar with the details—also speaking anonymously—called the price the province paid “crazy” and “a ridiculous amount of money,” especially for a property that would need to be rezoned before a school could be built.

“It’s a massive risk,” the source said, noting that Abbotsford has historically been reluctant to tweak its Official Community Plan to accommodate new uses within established zones.

Similarly, the province paid several times Farm Credit Canada’s reported regional average of $104,600 for agricultural parcels last year to acquire the farmland for the new Plant and Animal Health Centre. With farmland values in B.C. declining over the past 18 months, the province’s premium looks even more egregious.

While the purchase price was “well below” the prices of nearby retail or industrial properties, the site was purchased as actively farmed land within the Agricultural Land Reserve that would require a non-farm use application.

“Why the province paid so dearly for it, relative to what Panatch paid in 2020, is a bit of a mystery,” said Paul Richter, director of market analytics with CoStar. “They did go through the process to get ALC approval to subdivide into two parcels, and for ‘non-farm use’ approvals to permit the [Plant and Animal Health] Centre. This could have added value, for the right buyer. In this case, the only buyer that would have likely stepped up, stepped up. The province.”

The spending practices of other levels of government offer a point of comparison for the province’s land acquisitions.

The Department of National Defence acquired two multi-family properties on Vancouver Island last year to house personnel. A newly built 37-unit property at 244 Island Highway in View Royal traded in early October 2025 for $23.4 million, or an average of $631,622 per door unit—the most expensive multi-family transaction in Greater Victoria last year, according to CBRE Ltd. statistics.

Near CFB Comox, DND bought a 52-unit property at 574 Cumberland Rd., Courtenay, from Simba Investments Ltd. for $19.1 million. The purchase price averaged $367,308 a door—a premium versus the Mid-Island average at mid-year as reported by CBRE of $200,938 per door.

Within the Lower Mainland, the City of Coquitlam paid $3 million—or an average of $16.7 million per acre—in August 2025 for a 0.18-acre medium-density residential development site at 570 Austin Ave., Coquitlam.

The various government transactions, all completed within a few months of one another and involving different asset types, show a willingness to spend well beyond what the private sector would pay.

“It’s definitely a trend,” said the industry source familiar with the history of the Pratt Road site. “With half the developers I have done business with over the years, it’s well known that if they’re moving forward with a property, it’s because they’ve done their due diligence and they know that they can make money doing this. And they do that because they’re responsible for their own private capital and don’t want to lose money.”

Our typical listing spotlight features the standard bells and whistles, including savvy staging. But sometimes, all it takes to make the eyes (and heart) linger is a bare-bones set of photos and a strong foundation.

This is the case with 13 Euclid Avenue. Tucked north of Queen, just around the corner from Trinity Bellwoods Park, this duplex — asking $999,700 — hits the market with its upper levels presenting as a clean state. With no staging, renderings, or AI imaginings (phew), the home can’t hide.

But with quality craftsmanship, that's not a problem.

Across 2.5 storeys, multiple elements feel (and may just be) straight from a past era. On arrival, you’re met by original hardwood flooring, which continues to make appearances across other areas of the home (including the top-floor bedroom — more on that shortly).

Original millwork, detailed plaster ceilings that soar to generous heights, and large windows that fill the space with natural light all bring a special type of character that’s difficult to emulate in a new build.

    • Bedrooms: 4
    • Bathrooms: 2
    • Size: 1,500-2,000 sq. ft
    • Listed At: $999,700

The address is a working duplex; the lower unit — complete with its own kitchen and walkout to the backyard — is home to a tenant who, according to the listing, is happy to stay in place.

Make no mistake: there’s room for renovation and upgrades here, too. Whether it’s transforming the upper kitchen into an eat-in paradise, or combining landscaping with outdoor furniture to create a private backyard sanctuary, your imagination is the limit. But please, buyer-to-be — leave the blue bathroom tile intact.

We've already given the bathroom tile its flowers, so here we'll celebrate the main top-level bedroom. Spanning some half of the home's top floor, this room features hardwood planks that are wider than elsewhere in the home — and we're swooning over them. Pair that floor with the uniquely angular ceiling, a skylight, and the quirky shelf built into the wall, and you have the perfect place to design a primary-bedroom sanctuary. That, or a reading nook for the ages.

This address also comes complete with a detached garage off the laneway, a rare find for the area.

And speaking of the neighbourhood: beyond the craftsmanship, a key part of this home’s charm is its location — literal steps from the Queen West strip, calling 13 Euclid home would mean coffee at White Squirrel followed by a walk in the park as a daily routine. Sud Forno sandwiches would probably beckon most days, too. But we wouldn’t mind.

items.title: Empty homes tax debate swirls 10 years after pioneering tax in Vancouver
items.description: Developers warn the empty homes tax could increase costs and undermine new construction
items._ogDesc: Developers warn the empty homes tax could increase costs and undermine new construction
items.body:
The City of Vancouver launched a tax on empty dwellings 10 years ago that it billed as the first municipal tax of its kind anywhere in North America.

Debate swirls around how effective taxing empty homes is in helping the long-term housing market. This is despite even critics accepting that these taxes can help reduce the number of empty dwellings.

Since Vancouver introduced that initial empty homes tax, the concept has proved popular in public polling and among left-of-centre politicians that created similar themed taxes at the provincial and federal levels.

Governments roll out empty homes taxes over past decade

Gregor Robertson was Vancouver's mayor when he and his Vision Vancouver council approved the city's Empty Homes Tax (EHT) in November 2016. This came into effect Jan. 1, 2017.

Vancouver homeowners must submit an annual declaration so the city can determine whether their property is subject to the EHT.

Properties deemed or declared empty in 2025, for example, are subject to a three per cent tax on the property’s 2025 assessed value.

Former premier John Horgan and his NDP government were next to launch a tax on those who own vacant dwellings.

Enacted in 2018, the province's Speculation and Vacancy Tax (SVT) had its first declaration period for property owners in January and February 2019.

The SVT applies to municipalities across Metro Vancouver, the Capital Regional District in Greater Victoria and 26 other municipalities.

The province slaps a one per cent annual tax on Canadian citizens and permanent residents who own homes they leave vacant, while foreign residents who do that get a bigger tax bill, equal to three per cent of their property's assessed taxable value.

Former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's government introduced its Underused Housing Tax (UHT) to take effect in January 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government then earlier this year cancelled the UHT, saying the tax was costly and inefficient to administer, generating excessive compliance burdens and red tape for taxpayers.

Politicians promise new taxes on empty dwellings

Recent provincial and municipal election campaigns have provided further evidence of the popularity of the empty homes tax, particularly among left-of-centre politicians.

Former NDP MLA and Imagine Surrey leader Mike Starchuk, for example, promised during his recent failed mayoral campaign he would call on the provincial government to amend its Local Government Act to allow the City of Surrey create its own empty homes tax.

Vancouver was legally able to launch its pioneering EHT because it is governed by the Vancouver charter, which allows special taxing powers.

In contrast, the Local Government Act and Community Charter, which govern Surrey and other cities across the province, do not allow the same taxing powers.

Starchuk said he would apply his proposed municipal empty homes tax on dwellings left vacant for much of the year.

His intent is to reduce the asking price for new rents and help people find homes.

Starchuk said the initiative would also generate revenue to help fund affordable housing projects.

He is not alone in wanting to use taxation to help free up potential homes.

B.C. Premier David Eby, as NDP leader during the current election campaign, promised two separate measures to tax empty homes.

First, he pledged to introduce a new tax on condominiums that developers have completed but not sold.

This new condo tax would apply to finished units that have been left empty for more than a year and start at a two per cent rate.

The tax rate would then rise by one percentage point for each additional year that the units remain unsold and unoccupied, Eby said.

Eby explained the proposal in part by pointing to a Real Property Data report showing developers are sitting on about $4.4 billion worth of completed but empty homes.

Eby separately promised to increase the SVT’s rates to two per cent for domestic owners and to five per cent for foreign owners.

Number of empty homes fall in Vancouver after tax introduced

Reaction to the general concept of empty homes tax is mixed. Supporters point out evidence that the tax reduces the number of vacant homes. Others warn of unintended consequences and potential long-term harm to the housing market and economy.

Geoff Meggs, a Vision Vancouver councillor in the mid-2010s, told Business in Vancouver that he originally opposed the idea of bringing in an empty homes tax in Vancouver.

Vision Vancouver pushed for an empty homes tax while he was in office.

"I had reservations because it was not clear to me how big a problem it actually was," Meggs said.

Urban planning consultant Andy Yan had conducted a study of empty condominiums that used various data, including electricity consumption, to determine that Vancouver had a substantial number of vacant units.

Yan told BIV that his research focused on specific neighbourhoods in downtown Vancouver.

"The public was concerned because there were not enough lights on," Meggs said.

"But I wasn't sure how you could be sure that a place was empty, and therefore taxable. And how would you enforce it? I had all these questions, but we decided to do it because there was a lot of public concern."

He said his reticence turned out to be unfounded.

"The city was able to set up a system where people were required to disclose," he said. "It was quite simple. People had thought it would take forms that would go on forever, but it was a very straightforward online process that people declared and then people had to pay the tax."

Since the city implemented the tax, its data has shown a steady decline in the percentage of vacant homes in the city.

The city's annual report on the tax released last year showed, based on homeowner declarations, just 0.49 per cent of the homes in Vancouver are vacant—the lowest percentage since the tax launched.

That figure excludes vacant homes exempt from the tax because of fire damage, a court order restricting their use, a recent death or other reasons that the city considers valid.

The city's vacant home rate was 1.17 per cent in 2017, and in each successive year showed a decline.

In total, the number of vacant and exempted homes in Vancouver in 2024 was 4,697, or about 2.3 per cent of the city’s 201,739 total homes.

Of the other homes, 136,211 are principal residences and 60,831 are tenanted, according to the city.

Yan said he believes targeted taxes are effective at reducing the number of empty homes.

He pointed to a 2022 report by UBC economists Tsur Somerville and Jake Wetzel that found B.C.'s SVT has also been successful, returning approximately 20,000 vacant housing units to the long-term rental market in Metro Vancouver.

Taxes come with unintended consequences

Developers say taxes on vacant homes or on unsold inventory are misguided because they increase the cost of future development and can make projects financially unviable.

When developers get financing, they document their costs and risks and bring that to bankers, explained Michael Geller, a principal at Michael Geller Associates Ltd. and a longtime developer of small projects.

Higher costs and the risk of future taxes can force developers to take out larger loans and, in some cases, borrow at higher interest rates, he said.

One of Geller's main objections is that Vancouver's EHT is charged not only on empty homes, but also on empty development sites.

The city's rationale is that homeowners should not be able to avoid the tax by demolishing their dwellings, he explained.

The problem is that a development site can remain untouched because it is not financially viable for the owner to build homes and sell them at prices that cover costs and generate a profit, Geller said.

"The developer's permits may be held up," he added. "Maybe he can't arrange financing because there is no market. Meanwhile, in addition to his property taxes, he's now paying this empty homes tax that, one day, he'll have to try to recover from developing homes."

Geller also opposes Eby's promise to tax developers' unsold inventory of homes that have been vacant for more than a year.

Eby said at a news conference that B.C. needs this tax because developers are "hoarding" those units, waiting for them to go up in price.

"Nothing could be further from the truth," Geller told BIV. "The notion that they're hoarding them and keeping them off the market to maybe make them more valuable is preposterous."

The reality, he explained, is that lenders restrict developers' ability to sell the units.

Bankers almost always have clauses in lending agreements that set minimum prices at which developers are allowed to can sell units, he said.

If a developer sells a unit for below that set price, then the banker would require the developer to put in more capital of his or her own, Geller said.

He said bankers put these kinds of clauses in projects he developed, such as:

  • the four-unit Vinson House in West Vancouver;
  • the four-unit Ambleside Mews in West Vancouver; and
  • the 36-unit Elm Park Place in Vancouver.

Other developers stressed that developers are selling units as fast as they can.

Polygon Homes chairman Michael Audain told BIV that taxing empty homes or unsold condos is the "craziest idea I've ever heard."

He stressed that every completed condo that his company builds, it tries to sell as soon as it can. 

"We're not selling, certainly, at the rate that we were a few years ago, but we're selling everywhere at whatever the market will allow us to do because that's our business—to build and sell homes," he said. 

"There's no point putting a hammer on the developer to sell. The absorption can only be at a certain level, and demand is very low at the moment. You can't dump all your homes on the market at once."

Other developers told BIV that taxing developers for unsold inventory makes future development more costly, if not impossible.

"If the government is at all interested in encouraging housing development, this basically just shuts it down," Cressey Development Group executive vice-president Hani Lammam told BIV.

He said Cressey has no unsold inventory, although that could change this spring.

That is when Cressey expects to complete its 59-unit Rockford condominium project in Surrey, where 43 units were pre-sold.

Lammam said governments brought in empty homes taxes partly in response to the perception that wealthy foreign buyers owned B.C. homes as secondary residences.

"Circumstances have changed," Lammam said.

"There are no investors, virtually whatsoever, in the marketplace. The cost to produce the housing, when you aggregate all costs, is unaffordable for local incomes. So, the whole model is broken. Costs have to come down, or incomes have to go up."

Cressey has shifted over the past decade toward building more rental buildings and fewer condominium developments.

A tax on unsold inventory might push other developers to similarly shift toward building rental homes, Lammam said.

But he cautioned that building rental housing today is also challenging.

"Building rental was viable," he said. "Is it viable today, and are we starting new rental projects today? No, we're not because the costs are high and revenues are weak, and there's a flood of inventory."

That oversupply includes a major project by the Squamish First Nation, which has been able to build using different development requirements because the projects are on Squamish territory, he said.

The Squamish First Nation has finished the first phase of its Sen̓áḵw project at the south end of the Burrard Bridge—a development that has far less parking than the City of Vancouver would otherwise require.

That first phase delivered 1,409 units across three towers. When complete, Sen̓áḵw is expected to be the largest rental project in Vancouver's history, with 11 residential towers delivering providing more than 6,000 purpose-built rental homes.

The Musqueam First Nation is involved in East Wind near UBC which is expected to deliver 451 rental homes, including apartments and townhouses, by 2029.

items._ogDesc: The PBO projects Canada's federal borrowing will outpace deficits 2-to-1, with debt servicing costs exploding to consume 1 in 7 revenue dollars by 2030.
items.body:
Is it a bird? A plane? No, it’s… the size of Canada’s debt servicing costs. The Parliamentary Budget Officer’s (PBO) latest Economic and Fiscal Outlook projects Ottawa will accumulate $333 billion in deficit spending over 5 years. However, the Government of Canada (GoC) will need to borrow nearly three-quarters of a trillion dollars. Debt servicing is now the fastest-growing federal expense, projected to consume almost 1 in 7 dollars of revenue by 2030.

Federal Borrowing To Grow More Than 2x As Much As Deficits

Ottawa will accumulate $333.3 billion in cumulative deficits from 2026-27 through 2030-31. At the same time, the GoC will borrow an additional $732.9 billion, according to the PBO’s projections. That’s roughly 2.2 times as much borrowing than the projected deficit—or a deficit less than half the size of new borrowing. It depends on whether you’re a half-insolvent or half-solvent kind of person.

One of the reasons behind the gap is accounting methodology. Loans are both a liability and an asset; just think of it like a mortgage. One borrower’s liability of $100k is an asset of $100k to the lender. In this case, the gap is driven by Crown corporations and acquiring other assets. When the GoC borrows $1 billion and lends it to a Crown corporation, it owes investors $1 billion, but it’s also owed $1 billion. The loan doesn’t increase the deficit, just interest costs and any resulting losses.

It’s debatable whether it’s a good or bad decision, but the consequences are much clearer. “Most simply, cash outlays drive borrowing, which in turn increase market debt and public debt charges, independent of how they are recorded on an accrual basis,” warns the PBO.

The PBO’s calculations show a sharp impact on public finances in the coming years.

Canada To Spend Almost 1 In 7 Dollars of Revenue On Debt Payments

The PBO warns that debt charges are now the fastest-growing public expense. Annual public debt charges are projected to climb from $24.5 billion in 2021-22 to $59.3 billion in 2026-27. Their projections show it explodes to $83.0 billion in 2030-31, much faster than revenue. The PBO estimates debt repayment will consume 13.6% of revenue by 2030-31, up from 10.5% in 2025-26. Debt servicing is set to grow 29.5% faster than revenue, consuming almost 1 in 7 dollars collected.

Most are likely to assume this is due to higher interest rates, but that’s not what the numbers show. The PBO explains that this mainly reflects a larger stock of debt, not higher interest rates. That’s the fanciest way to say the captain of this ship didn’t realize they lost their anchor.

items.title: Canada’s Approved-But-Unstarted Homes Climb As Starts Slide
items.description:
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) counted 143,929 homes in September that have approved building permits and no construction started.

That count, reported alongside CMHC’s figures for centres of 50,000 or more, rose 1.1% from August.

Compared with a year ago, starts have fallen. Actual housing starts in centres of 10,000 or more were down 11% year-over-year in September, at 19,984 units compared with 22,375. From January through September, those centres recorded 170,964 starts, 4% behind the same period in 2025.

“As outlined in CMHC’s latest Housing Supply Report (HSR), a key risk for Canada now is not building enough during this period of softening housing markets across the country,” said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at CMHC.

“Canada still faces a long-term housing supply gap and unless housing construction levels increase, improvements in housing affordability since 2023 will be difficult to sustain,” he said.

Right now, starts are down from last year.

The headline figures make that harder to see: the seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of starts across Canada rose 3% in September, to 248,896 units from 242,223 in August. CMHC’s six-month trend, a moving average of that rate, barely budged, and landed at 250,411.

CMHC uses the trend alongside the monthly SAAR to account for considerable swings in the monthly figure. Multi-unit starts largely drive the market, and they can vary widely from one month to the next.

Homes already underway are holding steady. There were 371,617 units under construction in centres of 50,000 or more in September, flat from August. Completions fell 0.9% to 17,398 units.

The regional picture is uneven. “Of Canada’s four most populous provinces, only Quebec has seen modest gains in housing starts for 2026 and each of the seven major centres covered in the HSR are behind 2025’s pace for new home construction,” ab Iorwerth said.

Montreal’s six-month trend fell 8% in September on lower multi-unit starts. Vancouver’s rose 6% on higher multi-unit starts. Toronto’s was flat, with single-detached and multi-unit trends offsetting each other.

CMHC will release October’s housing starts data on November 17.

items._ogDesc: September Canadian inflation breached the BoC target at 3.1%. Regional CPI data reveals only Ontario and BC are below the national average.
items.body:
The August Consumer Price Index (CPI) report breached the Bank of Canada (BoC) upper bound. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows CPI accelerated further in September. A regional breakdown reveals that only two provinces are below the national average. Headline growth is well above the BoC’s target rate, but some provinces have more than doubled that rate.

Canadian Inflation Accelerates, Already Past BoC Upper Bound

Canadian CPI annual growth.

Annual growth of CPI accelerated to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August. The outsized impact of soaring gas prices continues, with CPI ex-gasoline at just 2.2% over the same period. The agency further notes that only 3 of 8 major components saw prices accelerate too.

The headline data makes it easy to conclude this is only an energy story. However, a regional breakdown of CPI makes it clear that basket distortions are in play. Only two provinces have seen a rate lower than the national average.

Atlantic Provinces Over 2x BoC Target, Only 2 Provinces Below Average

Despite being above the Bank of Canada (BoC) upper bound of 3.0%, CPI may be skewed by its modelling. A quick look at the provincial breakdowns, and we see Ontario (+2.5%) is the only province below the threshold. Add BC (+3.0%) to the mix, and we get the only two provinces lower than the national average. The rest of Canada isn’t quite this lucky—especially out east.

CPI’s highest growth is almost exclusively concentrated in Atlantic Canada. PEI’s annual growth of 5.7%—approaching triple the BoC’s target of 2%—is the highest in the country. Not far behind are Nova Scotia (+5.6%), New Brunswick (+5.0%), and Newfoundland and Labrador (+4.7%). The Prairies aren’t much better off either—Manitoba (+4.4%), Alberta (+3.6%), and Saskatchewan (+3.3%) are above the national average too.

It’s not just gas, either. CPI ex-gasoline remained elevated in Nova Scotia (+4.4%), PEI (+3.9%), and New Brunswick (+3.4%). The agency separately notes “… rent prices rose the fastest in Atlantic Canada,” which can help explain some of the distortion.

Energy and Shelter Are Among The Biggest Drivers of CPI

The biggest driver of annual growth remains energy, with 19% annual growth. The sector is driven by a 27.8% surge in gas, along with a 57.8% jump in fuel oil. Considering energy is an input cost for everything, its surprising growth isn’t broad.

Shelter accelerated 1.8%, driven by home/mortgage insurance (+4.9%) and rent (+2.8%). The sector was moderated by falling replacement costs (-1.9%), tied to the cost of building new homes. It was dragged further by mortgage interest (-0.2%), which is likely to be news to brokers considering yields.

In short, Canada’s headline inflation is running hot—and the national average is weak in contrast to what most households are experiencing.

items.title: Ahead Of BC Election, UDI, Housing Central Push For Four Actions
items.description:
On October 13, the Urban Development Institute (UDI), BC Non-Profit Housing Association (BCNPHA), Aboriginal Housing Management Association (AHMA), and Co-operative Housing Federation of BC (CHFBC) — the latter three of which are together known as Housing Central — published a joint news release “calling on every party in the provincial election to commit to bringing down the cost of building homes” as Election Day nears.

UDI is the group that lobbies on behalf of private developers while the Housing Central partners represent the non-profits, Indigenous housing providers, and co-ops in the community housing sector.

Because of their different focuses, the two groups are often on opposite sides of housing debates, hence why they described themselves as “unlikely allies.” They say they are coming together now because they have all reached the same conclusion: “neither sector can build at today’s costs and within an uncertain regulatory and funding environment.”

“The cost of building and financing a home in BC now exceeds what most buyers can afford to pay and what governments are willing to subsidize for low- and moderate-income renters,” the alliance said in their news release. “For market and non-market builders alike, this means projects that don't pencil and never get off the drawing board.”

With Budget 2026 earlier this year, the Province said they were adjusting the pacing of $1.4 billion in planned housing investments, which notably included an abrupt pause pertaining to the Community Housing Fund, which has stranded numerous non-profit housing projects and become a sore spot for the sector.

The groups say over 5,000 affordable rental units have been impacted, and project proponents have lost $45 million in pre-development costs.

After the Governments of Canada and Ontario announced an $8.8 billion deal this spring to cut development charges and eliminate the 13% HST on housing, the development industry in BC started pushing for a similar deal.

While the Governments of Canada and British Columbia finally made an announcement in June, it included a similar deal to cut development charges, but there was nothing on eliminating the GST, with the Province saying they were uninterested in it despite recognizing that the industry had been pushing for it.

In their joint news release, UDI and the Housing Central partners noted that the agreement to reduce development charges was not finalized before Premier David Eby called a snap election on September 22, and thus builders still cannot price it into their projects.

The alliance called for four actions to address the above points:

  1. Restoring the planned investments into non-profit, co-op and Indigenous housing so that the development of 5,000 affordable homes can get back on track.
  2. Finalize a commitment to co-invest remaining BC Rental Protection Funds with the Canada Rental Protection Fund to continue protecting the affordability that already exists in the market and provide housing stability for thousands of tenants across BC.
  3. Finalizing the federal-provincial agreement on development cost charges and infrastructure within [90] days of forming government, so DCC reductions reach projects on the ground.
  4. Following Ontario’s lead by securing a GST exemption on new homes for all buyers, not only first-time buyers.

“The projects are ready, but the land sits empty,” said BCNPHA CEO Jill Atkey. “The people waiting for affordable housing cannot wait another budget cycle. The next government has an opportunity to restore the investment and get these homes built.”

“When market developers and non-profit housing providers are asking for the same thing, it should tell every party how serious the cost of delivery crisis is,” added UDI CEO Mike Drummond.

Housing has not been as front-and-centre compared to the election in 2024, with this election’s primary focuses being Eby’s record and decision to call the election, the economy, and BC’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA).

The most substantial commitment on the housing front has been Eby and the NDP’s proposed Unsold Condo Tax on completed unsold inventory, which has drawn widespread criticism from the industry.

Election Day is Saturday, October 24.

items.title: Down payment rules outdated, says credit union CEO
items.description: Beem's Brian Harris urges greater emphasis on financial behaviour
items._ogDesc: Beem's Brian Harris urges greater emphasis on financial behaviour
items.body:
With housing costs and living expenses remaining high in B.C., people struggling to save for a down payment shouldn't be shut out of homeownership, says the CEO of a major credit union.

Brian Harris, president and CEO of Beem Credit Union, said down payments have become an “outdated” primary measure of a person’s readiness for homeownership, an argument that at least one housing expert disputes.

“If you think about the fact that people are saving money anywhere from three to nine years to get into homeownership, that's a lot of money tied up in rental that could have otherwise been much more constructively used,” said Harris.

“I just think it's a really outdated way of determining worthiness and readiness for homeownership.”

About one-third (32 per cent) of Canadians said saving for a down payment was their main barrier to entering the housing market, according to a 2025 survey by CPA Canada and BDO Debt Solutions.

A September survey by Royal LePage also found that more than half of the 1,400 newcomers surveyed across Canada cited saving for a down payment as their biggest barrier for homeownership.

Harris said a family in Metro Vancouver could pay $5,000 a month in rent—an amount that could be comparable to the monthly mortgage payment on a home worth roughly $1 million, depending on the financing terms.

Rather than using down payment as a predominant criterion, Harris said lenders could take a more thoughtful and creative approach to evaluating mortgage applicants by considering their credit history, spending habits and track record of rental payment.

“We have consumer-directed finance, or open banking, as it’s more affectionately referred to, coming to Canada, so we have the ability in the very near term to have really good data insights to determine how somebody is spending their money,” he said.

Canada’s consumer-driven banking framework is designed to allow consumers to share their financial data securely with accredited third-party providers of their choice. The federal government has established the legislative framework and is developing supporting regulations to put it into operation.

“There's a real opportunity for us to use demonstrated behaviours and other sort of support tools to get people in [if] they've exhibited good financial behaviours,” said Harris.

He said a more flexible approach to mortgage qualification could also benefit the broader housing market by matching the demand for homeownership with accessibility.

“I think it's got a lot of great knock-on effects. It gets people who are renting into whatever form it takes, a small home, a condo, a townhouse, whatever it might be,” said Harris.

“But it then also frees up the rental market for those who are not yet ready to buy their own home.”

Down payment requirements still matter

While a down payment is not the only indicator of someone’s readiness for homeownership, removing the requirement could increase risks for both lenders and buyers, according to one real estate expert.

“The benefits of having a down payment, both in terms of an indication that the borrower's capable of making ongoing payments or de-risking the loan for the lender, I think are still true,” said Thomas Davidoff, an associate professor and director for UBC Centre for Urban Economics and Real Estate.

He said one of the main benefits of requesting a down payment is that it makes it harder for the buyer to get to a situation where the property is worth less than what the borrower owes, so they may walk away and stop paying the mortgage.

The ability to save for a down payment remains an important indicator of a person’s capability to save, alongside a good credit history, he said. However, he acknowledged that it is harder than it used to be to save for a down payment due to housing affordability issues in the region.

“If the money comes from the parents, less so, but on the other hand … that indicates you have [supportive] parents, which is helpful,” he said.

A down payment also reduces the amount a buyer needs to borrow, lowering monthly mortgage payments and borrowing costs, Davidoff added.

In addition, the current housing downturn indicates that property prices could fall, making high loan-to-value mortgages riskier, he said.

The key to tackling housing affordability is not in changing mortgage qualification rules, but lies in increasing the supply and growing the economy to boost people’s incomes and purchasing power, according to Davidoff.

“Higher earnings, more houses, that's the recipe,” he said.

“Make sure people are more able to earn a strong income with better education and a stronger labour market, more employers, so things like trade diversification in the face of U.S. tariffs, anything like that helps.”

items.title: Metro Vancouver home prices drop 4% in Q3 as Royal LePage forecasts further decline
items.description: Trade uncertainty keeps Metro Vancouver homebuyers on sidelines, says the brokage
items._ogDesc: Trade uncertainty keeps Metro Vancouver homebuyers on sidelines, says the brokage
items.body:
Metro Vancouver home prices continued to fall in the third quarter as economic uncertainty and concerns about future borrowing costs kept buyers on the sidelines, according to a new report from Royal LePage.

The aggregate home price in Metro Vancouver, which tracks price trends across different types of homes, declined four per cent year-over-year and 1.4 per cent from the previous quarter in the third quarter of 2026, according to the brokerage’s latest House Price Survey and Market Forecast, released Oct. 15.

Royal LePage forecasts the region’s aggregate home price will fall a further 4.5 per cent year-over-year in the fourth quarter.

“The Vancouver housing market hasn’t come to a total standstill, but it is operating well below normal levels, with transaction volumes consistently running 25 to 30 per cent below our 10-year average,” said Randy Ryalls, managing broker at Royal LePage Sterling Realty, in a statement.

“Sales activity steadily declined over the summer months and into the start of fall, and while inventory tightened slightly, it hasn't been enough to keep prices from declining.”

The median price of a single-family detached home in Metro Vancouver fell 5.6 per cent year-over-year to nearly $1.62 million, while the median condo price declined 4.1 per cent year-over-year to $712,100.

Nationally, the aggregate home price fell 0.8 per cent year-over-year to $810,000, while the median condo price declined 1.5 per cent to $571,900.

Phil Soper, Royal LePage president and CEO, said renewed trade tensions between Canada and the U.S. have weighed on consumer confidence, making prospective buyers more hesitant to commit to major purchases.

Concerns that mortgage rates could rise are also keeping would-be buyers on the sidelines, he added.

“The opportunity is there; the confidence to act remains elusive,” said Soper in a statement.

“With more homes to choose from and little pressure to act quickly, buyers can afford to wait—and uncertainty gives them a reason to.”

According to Royal LePage’s 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey, 45 per cent of Vancouver homeowners with a mortgage on their primary residence expect their monthly payments to increase when they renew.

Household debt is adding to financial pressures, as non-mortgage debt reached $712.2 billion in the second quarter, up 4.8 per cent year-over-year, according to figures cited in the report.

“It’s created a stop-and-start environment, where momentum never really takes off and pricing strategy is everything,” said Ryalls, adding that some sellers are pulling properties off the market if they’re not desperate to sell, while homes that are “aggressively priced” still attract multiple offers.

Despite forecasting a further decline in Metro Vancouver, Royal LePage expects Canada’s aggregate home price to increase one per cent year-over-year in the fourth quarter of 2026.

items.title: Expert: Canada’s Homes Got Cheaper In September, But Buyers Still Pulled Back
items.description:
Canadian homes got cheaper in September. Buyers responded by purchasing fewer of them. A falling price is welcome, but it does little for a household whose mortgage approval no longer covers the home.

There were 36,657 residential sales in September, 7.7% fewer than a year earlier. Sales fell 2.3% from August after seasonal adjustment, so the decline went beyond the usual seasonal change.

September residential sales, not seasonally adjusted; the annual comparison uses CREA’s revised figures. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

The national benchmark price fell 0.4% during September and was 3.4% below a year earlier. The average sale price fell 1.6% annually to $666,538. The benchmark tracks comparable housing attributes; the average also changes with the mix of homes sold.

Annual changes in the unadjusted national MLS® HPI and average sale price. The average is affected by the mix of transactions. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

A discount can disappear into the mortgage

CREA blames the weaker outlook on another increase in fixed mortgage rates and uncertainty over how far variable rates may rise. Its October forecast points to renewed energy-related inflation risks and a more hawkish Bank of Canada. The assumption of an easy return to cheaper borrowing has become harder to defend.

A buyer can negotiate thousands off the purchase price and still face a payment they cannot carry. How much of the discount survives depends on the mortgage size, rate and amortization. The asking price has come down; the lender has not necessarily become more generous.

There is more scope to negotiate than there was during the boom, but national listings are hardly overflowing. CREA counted slightly more than 200,000 homes for sale at the end of September, up just 1.8% annually and close to the historical norm.

B.C.’s supply problem looks different from Manitoba’s

Canada had 4.9 months of inventory after seasonal adjustment. British Columbia had 7.0 months, Manitoba 2.4, and Saskatchewan 3.4. Ontario was at 4.7. The ratio compares the stock of listings with the current sales pace.

Seasonally adjusted residential months of inventory by province. Local property types can differ substantially. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Ontario’s sales-to-new-listings ratio was only 41.9%, even with fewer months of inventory than B.C. The first ratio compares purchases with new listings arriving that month. Months of inventory compares the stock already available with the current sales pace.

A buyer shopping for an apartment can face much less competition than someone looking for a detached home in the same city. Provincial totals are a poor substitute for checking the homes that actually fit the budget.

Ontario is doing worse than the national forecast

CREA forecasts a 0.2% increase in the national annual average sale price to $681,681 in 2026. Ontario’s average is forecast to fall 3% to $809,334, and B.C.’s to fall 0.8%. Gains elsewhere keep the national number slightly positive.

Ontario and B.C. are the two provinces with forecast annual average-price declines in 2026. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Newfoundland and Labrador has the strongest expected average-price growth this year at 5.7%, followed by Saskatchewan at 5%. CREA expects both to slow in 2027, to 3.1% and 2.5% respectively.

The national average is projected to reach $689,909 in 2027, up 1.2%. Ontario’s forecast gain is 0.7%, to $815,100. These are nominal annual averages. Ontario’s projected increase next year would recover only a small part of this year’s forecast loss.

Annual average transaction prices in Canadian dollars. Forecast values are not December price targets. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Five years later, parts of Ontario are still cheaper

Greater Toronto’s September benchmark was 14.7% below its September 2021 level. Hamilton-Burlington was down 15.3%. Calgary was 24.6% higher, Quebec City 54.4% higher and St. John’s 41.2% higher. These are seasonally adjusted composite benchmarks measured from September 2021, before the 2022 peak.

Five-year changes in seasonally adjusted composite MLS® HPI benchmarks, September 2021 to September 2026. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

For an owner in one of the weaker Ontario markets, waiting has already failed to guarantee a better sale price. Moving can mean accepting less equity than expected while financing the next purchase at a higher rate. That is a good reason for a household to stay put, even when it would rather move.

Developers also have to compete with the prices buyers can pay for existing homes. Softer resale prices can squeeze the revenue available to cover a new project’s costs. CREA’s releases do not track presales, construction costs, or developer balance sheets, so they cannot tell us which projects will proceed.

Pent-up demand still needs a mortgage

CREA now expects 444,530 sales in 2026 and 464,235 in 2027. The forecast rebound of 4.4% would leave annual sales 4,436 below 2025. Even the recovery scenario falls short of that earlier year’s activity.

The confident pitch about pent-up demand has become harder to hear over repeated forecast cuts. CREA still uses the term in its 2027 outlook, but buyers are expected to return after economic growth, renewed population growth and a clearer interest-rate path help them along. Calling demand pent-up does not make it financeable.

That forecast also assumes limited further action by the Bank of Canada. September showed how quickly higher borrowing costs can interrupt a recovery. Buyers may get a better price this fall, but they still have to live with the payment.

Annual forecast prices are nominal transaction averages; forecasts are scenarios, not observed outcomes.

Monthly statistics: https://stats.crea.ca/en-ca/

items.title: Bank of Canada Board launches process to fill external Deputy Governor position
items.description: The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor.
items._ogDesc: The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor.
items.body:
The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor. The Board has formed a selection committee and retained recruitment firm Egon Zehnder to assist with the search process.

“The Bank has been operating in a rapidly changing and shock-prone economic environment, amid heightened uncertainty and longer-term structural change” said Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem. “It’s more important than ever to bring in policymakers with fresh perspectives and a diverse set of skills.”

The Bank created the role of external Deputy Governor in 2022 with the goal of bringing fresh and diverse perspectives to strengthen its monetary policy deliberations and financial stability assessments. External Deputy Governor appointments are part-time roles for a two-year term, with the possibility of extension for an additional one or two years. During their terms, external Deputy Governors contribute directly to the formulation of monetary policy, the assessment of financial stability risks, and the development of the Bank's strategic thinking on economic and financial matters. They also play an important role in the Bank's communications and outreach activities.

“As members of Governing Council, external Deputy Governors have demonstrated their value in bringing complementary experience and expertise to the table,” said Anne Whelan, Lead Independent Director. “The successful candidate will have the opportunity to further enrich Governing Council deliberations and contribute directly to economic and financial policy decisions affecting Canadians.”

The Bank’s selection committee is seeking outstanding candidates from a broad range of disciplines and backgrounds, with extensive senior-level experience in economics, finance, financial markets or related fields and the ability to assess and communicate complex economic and financial issues. Interested candidates are encouraged to review the Executive Brief for the role and contact Egon Zehnder to discuss their candidacy at: ExternalDG-SGexterne@egonzehnder.com

items.title: Bank of Canada unveils new vertical $20 bank note
items.description: Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III.
items._ogDesc: Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III.
items.body:
Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III. This is Canada’s first bank note to feature His Majesty’s portrait and the first time in more than 70 years that a new monarch has appeared on the $20 denomination. The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.

“This new $20 bank note is striking, symbolic and secure,” said Governor Macklem. “The note’s advanced and dynamic security features are combined with images that reflect Canada’s beauty and its history. I hope it evokes pride in Canada and confidence in its bank notes.”

The portrait of his Majesty is surrounded by a floral and leafy tapestry inspired by the King’s lifetime dedication to the environment. The back of the note retains the Canadian National Vimy Memorial in France as a tribute to Canada’s contributions and sacrifices in military conflicts throughout its history.

Provincial and territorial floral emblems representing the 13 provinces and territories appear on the front of the note. A circular window, visible from both sides of the note, features plants that are culturally significant to Indigenous Peoples in Canada. The Bank’s Indigenous Advisory Circle collaborated on creating the design of this window.

This is the second bank note in the Vertical series. The first, the $10 note, features civil rights pioneer and businesswoman Viola Desmond.

The Bank also consulted with Canadians, government partners and a range of stakeholders including accessibility groups and organizations connected to the memorial at Vimy Ridge. Their input was instrumental in the development of the new $20 note.

Bank note security is integral to Canada’s currency and to the confidence of consumers and businesses that rely on cash. The new $20 note has security features never before used on Canadian currency that are easy to check and hard to counterfeit. The purple security stripe includes elements that spin, transform and pulse when the note is moved. Features like these will help the Bank maintain its technical advantage over counterfeiters and enable Canadians to easily authenticate $20 bank notes, the denomination they use most often. This ensures Canadians can use the new $20 note with confidence.

“The new $20 note reflects important parts of who we are as Canadians, honouring our Commonwealth roots and our ties with international allies,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “It honours our constitutional traditions through the portrait of His Majesty King Charles III and recognizes the service and sacrifice of Canadians through the Vimy Memorial, a symbol that continues to resonate across generations.”

“The new $20 bank note tells a distinctly Canadian story—one shaped by our natural beauty, our rich history and the enduring partnerships we have built around the world,” said Secretary of State Long. “It is a symbol Canadians can carry with pride.”

Before issuing the new note, the Bank will raise awareness among the public and other stakeholders. When introducing new notes, the Bank works closely with financial institutions, equipment manufacturers and the cash-handling industry to help ease the transition. This includes encouraging businesses that use bank note handling and processing equipment to contact their suppliers about any necessary machine adaptations. Retailers, law enforcement agencies and others will also be informed about the note’s design and security features, helping to maintain Canadians’ trust in their bank notes.

Remarks

Read the full remarks delivered during the unveiling of the new $20 bank note in Ottawa.

  • Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem
  • Governor General Louise Arbour

  • For more information on the visual elements and security features of the new $20 bank note, visit our website or watch the video. Find conceptual images of the new note on Flickr.
  • Read about our principles for bank note design.
  • Visit our bank notes page for information and resources on past and current Canadian bank notes.

items.description: The Bank of Canada today held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada today held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada today held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%.

The continuing conflict in the Middle East is keeping energy prices high. As well, new US tariffs and Canadian counter-measures have been announced following the breakdown of trade talks between Canada and the United States. Both situations remain fluid.

In the United States, economic growth continues to be solid, driven by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Growth in the euro area was stronger than expected in the second quarter, while China’s economy slowed. Overall, the global economy has shown resilience in the face of geopolitical headwinds, with growth broadly consistent with the July Monetary Policy Report (MPR) projection. With still-high oil prices and elevated margins for refined energy products, inflation in most countries remains high.

Financial conditions have tightened since July. Long-term bond yields have moved up globally, including in Canada. The Canadian dollar has appreciated slightly on US-dollar weakness.

As expected, Canadian economic activity strengthened in the second quarter, with GDP up by 3.3%, following very weak growth in the first quarter. While some of the recent strength reflected temporary factors, the pick-up in activity was broad-based. Consumption showed solid gains. Following several weak quarters, there was some rebound in housing activity. Exports and business investment were up sharply. Labour market conditions have improved in recent months, with the unemployment rate edging down to 6.4% in July. Still, demand for labour remains subdued and indicators point to continued excess supply in the economy.

Overall, recent data reaffirm Governing Council’s view of a broadening recovery in Canada’s economy. However, uncertainty is high and new US tariffs and threats of further action pose risks to the sustainability of the recovery.

CPI inflation has been hovering around 3% in recent months, mainly because of persistently higher gasoline prices. So far, there has been little evidence of higher energy prices spreading to other components of inflation: excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2% and measures of core inflation remained close to 2% in July. However, with the Middle East conflict still ongoing and little progress reopening the Strait of Hormuz, upside risks to the Bank’s inflation forecast have increased. The longer that high oil prices and elevated refinery margins persist, the greater the risk of spillover to the prices of other goods and services. New US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs will also raise costs for some businesses and could feed into consumer prices over time.

With the economy and inflation evolving broadly as forecast in the July MPR, Governing Council agreed to leave the policy rate unchanged. However, the upside risks to inflation have increased, while new tariffs make growth prospects more uncertain. Governing Council will assess the sustainability of the economic rebound and the outlook for inflation, and is prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed. The Bank remains committed to maintaining Canadians’ confidence in price stability through this period of global upheaval.

The next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is October 28, 2026. The Bank’s next MPR will be released at the same time.

items.title: G7 2026 Cross-Border Coordination Exercise (CBCE)
items.description: The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector.
items._ogDesc: The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector.
items.body:
The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector. A long-term exercise strategy has now been adopted to increase the frequency and consistency of these simulations, thereby enhancing preparedness across all jurisdictions.

Building on the success of the 2024 CBCE exercise, which aimed to strengthen the G7 financial authorities’ capacity to coordinate and communicate effectively in response to a major cross-border cyber incident affecting the financial sector, this year’s sessions tested key improvements identified through previous simulations and workshops focused on incident response, recovery, and crisis communication, further advancing collective preparedness. To enhance coordination among G7 financial authorities, the exercise simulated a large-scale cyber-attack across all G7 jurisdictions. The scenario brought together ministries of finance, central banks, bank supervisors, and market authorities, fostering a unified response.

Through these exercises, the G7 Cyber Expert Group seeks to reinforce the financial sector’s capacity to withstand cyber threats and reduce potential disruptions across G7 jurisdictions.

“As cyber threats continue to evolve, cooperation across G7 nations is more important than ever. Exercises such as this one strengthen our collective ability to respond to major cyber incidents, improve information sharing among financial authorities, and reinforce the resilience of the global financial system. I thank all participants for their continued commitment to this important work.”
- The Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue

This initiative enables financial authorities to further align and integrate the various operational and strategic components required for an effective response to cyber incidents.

In an increasingly interconnected world, cross-border coordination, incident response preparedness, and timely information sharing remain key G7 priorities. The G7 Cyber Expert Group continues to work and collaborate to address potential cyber threats to safeguard the stability and integrity of the global financial system.

“In our increasingly global financial system, countries can't address cyberthreats in isolation. Cross-border coordination exercises allow us to test and align our cyber security preparedness with domestic and international partners. This improves our resilience - both individually and collectively.”
- Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada

About the G7 Cyber Expert Group

The G7 Cyber Expert Group is responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy and strategy across the G7 jurisdictions. Its mission is to enhance the cyber resilience of the financial sector by fostering preparedness, establishing a shared understanding of the threat landscape, and promoting unified approaches to risk mitigation.

Recent G7 Cyber Expert Group publications include:

  • G7 Cyber Expert Group Statement on AI and Cybersecurity (2025)
  • G7 CEG Reconnection Framework Best Practice (2025)
  • G7 Cyber Expert Group statement on transition to post-quantum cryptography (2026)

items.title: Bank of Canada publishes report on  monetary policy framework consultations
items.description: The Bank of Canada today published a report summarizing the feedback it received from stakeholders and the Canadian public during consultations on its monetary policy framework.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada today published a report summarizing the feedback it received from stakeholders and the Canadian public during consultations on its monetary policy framework.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada today published a report summarizing the feedback it received from stakeholders and the Canadian public during consultations on its monetary policy framework.

Every five years, the Bank of Canada and the Government of Canada review and renew the agreement on Canada’s monetary policy framework. The agreement will be renewed before the end of 2026. In preparation, the Bank held consultations to gather views on inflation, monetary policy and on three key challenges to Canada’s economy that were the focus of the Bank’s research.

  • In a world with more adverse supply shocks affecting inflation dynamics and economic activity, how should monetary policy respond?
  • In a world more prone to volatility, how should the Bank assess and communicate about inflation? What measures of core inflation are most robust to structural changes in the economy?
  • How does monetary policy affect housing demand and supply, and how is inflation in shelter prices measured and interpreted for policy purposes?

Conversations were held in communities across the country to better understand Canadians’ recent experience with inflation and to hear their perspectives on monetary policy. The Bank also met with a broad group of stakeholders including members of the research community, the private sector and civil society.

The feedback the Bank received indicates that Canadians value the stability the framework provides. Support for maintaining flexible inflation targeting and the 2% inflation target was strong. At the same time, many participants expressed concerns about the high cost of living and housing affordability. They indicated that clear communication about the information the Bank uses to make interest rate decisions is key to fostering trust in the central bank.

“It was important for the Bank to hear from Canadians as part of this process because inflation and interest rate decisions affect their day-to-day lives,” said Governor Tiff Macklem. “I’m thankful to everyone who participated in these consultations and for the value these perspectives will bring to the renewal of our policy framework.”

items.title: Bank of Canada joins BIS Project Agorá to test improvements in wholesale cross-border payments
items.description: The Bank of Canada announced today it is joining the Bank for International Settlements’ Project Agorá, an initiative exploring how tokenization could improve wholesale cross-border payments.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada announced today it is joining the Bank for International Settlements’ Project Agorá, an initiative exploring how tokenization could improve wholesale cross-border payments.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada announced today it is joining the Bank for International Settlements’ Project Agorá, an initiative exploring how tokenization could improve wholesale cross-border payments.

The project has successfully tested the feasibility of a multi-currency unified ledger that enables atomic settlement of cross-border wholesale transactions. The Agorá prototype combines tokenized commercial bank deposits and wholesale central bank money on a programmable platform with the aim of improving the speed, efficiency, transparency and accessibility of international payments.

The project will continue to test the prototype and examine how an Agorá-type platform could operate within existing legal and regulatory frameworks, including rules on settlement finality as well as laws designed to counter money-laundering and terrorism financing.

Project Agorá brings together central banks and private sector financial institutions to experiment with next-generation payments infrastructure. It aligns with the Bank of Canada’s research focus on the evolution of payments and how emerging technologies can support a more efficient financial system.

“We know that the Canadian economy could benefit from innovation in cross-border payments,” said Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers. “Tokenization has the potential to make these payments faster, cheaper and more efficient and secure. Project Agorá is a unique opportunity to test the technology across several jurisdictions and currencies, with the participation of private sector financial institutions.”

The global project involves seven other central banks—the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Bank of England, Bank of France (representing the Eurosystem), Bank of Japan, Bank of Mexico, Swiss National Bank and Bank of Korea—and involves more than 40 financial institutions, including systemically important banks, payment service providers and clearing houses.

items.title: Bank of Canada Museum honours two Canadian educators for innovation in the classroom
items.description: Ethan McDonagh and Andrew Leong have won the Bank of Canada Museum’s 2026 Award for Excellence in Teaching Economics.
items._ogDesc: Ethan McDonagh and Andrew Leong have won the Bank of Canada Museum’s 2026 Award for Excellence in Teaching Economics.
items.body:
Ethan McDonagh and Andrew Leong have won the Bank of Canada Museum’s 2026 Award for Excellence in Teaching Economics. McDonagh is a Wilfrid Laurier University student completing a practicum at Northbrae Public School in London, Ontario. Leong teaches at Prince of Wales Secondary School in Vancouver, British Columbia.

They were chosen from nominations across Canada for lessons that helped students connect economics to contemporary issues. “What impressed the selection committee was how intentionally these lessons were designed for real-world understanding,” said Deputy Governor Sharon Kozicki. “Whether students were visualizing income distribution with beads or ‘travelling’ through global economies, the learning was active, inquiry-based and grounded in evidence. That’s what great economics education looks like.”

Ethan McDonagh (Grade 6, London, ON)

McDonagh designed an inquiry-based Grade 6 lesson that used coloured beads as data to explore income distribution, the value of labour and fairness. Working in pairs, students allocated 100 beads across 10 professions to show what they believed people should earn, then combined their results into a visual model. McDonagh then introduced gold beads representing actual Canadian income distribution for the same professions. Students compared their “should earn” models with the real data by graphing the two and calculating mean, median and mode. Using the poverty line as a reference point, students then had a rich discussion about basic needs and fairness. The class concluded with an $8 million redistribution challenge that asked students to defend their decisions.

Andrew Leong (Grade 12, Vancouver, BC)

Leong created a gamified project, called the Macroeconomic Venture Passport, that helps Grade 12 students learn macroeconomics by “travelling” through eight global economies and earning passport stamps. Each stop uses hands-on activities and simulations to explore real issues shaping today’s economies—such as artificial intelligence and automation in Japan, deforestation in the Amazon and Canada’s 2% inflation target. Students also tackled fiscal trade-offs through a budget-balancing game, seeing how policy choices can affect debt and everyday costs. By blending storytelling, data and mini-challenges, Leong helped students connect abstract macroeconomic concepts to daily life and understand Canada’s place in an interconnected global economy.

Each winner receives a trophy along with a personal cash prize of $1,000 and another $1,000 for their school.

Nominations for next year’s award will open in early 2027.
